title: Modeling the Microenvironmental Dynamics of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma in Lacrimal Gland with Treatment Intervention
summary: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the lacrimal gland is a rare and extremely life threatening malignant tumor with a high risk of recurrence and poor long-term outcomes. On the other hand, due to its complex molecular dynamics and low incidence rate, treatment strategies are very limited. In this study, a mathematical model is developed based on the biological phenomena of the tumor microenvironment using nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It is analyzed both analytically and numerically. According to the findings, the growth of tumor cells is associated with the depletion of oxygen and nutrients, while severe hypoxia promotes the development of abnormal blood vessels and makes tumor control more difficult. Surgery and postoperative radiotherapy have been considered as treatment strategies, and we have observed that surgery alone may not be sufficient to prevent the regrowth of residual tumor cells. In addition, postoperative radiotherapy provides better control of the residual tumor burden, particularly when the remaining tumor cells have higher radiosensitivity. Furthermore, different radiotherapy interruption scenarios have been investigated, and the results indicate that longer gaps between radiotherapy doses can adversely affect the overall treatment response, leading to increased overall toxicity and a higher number of residual tumor cells at the end of the observation period. Consequently, our results suggest that postoperative radiotherapy after surgery, combined with adequate radiosensitivity of the residual tumor cells and adherence to the prescribed treatment schedule without prolonged interruptions, may reduce the risk of tumor recurrence and potentially improve long term survival.

title: Sense-Making phase transition framework for Affect
summary: Contemporary accounts of affect emphasize different perspectives, ranging from the regulation of bodily states in allostatic approaches to the relational and sense-making character stressed by enactive theories. Here, we show that affect can be made explicit within the sense-making phase transition framework previously introduced for the perception of an inner sensation. Within this same formal structure, each stable minimum of the sense-making potential defines an affective state: its position determines valence, while its depth determines arousal. Affect therefore is not introduced as an independent ingredient, but emerges as the associated state in the valence-arousal space, providing a link between allostatic and enactive approaches to affect. This formulation distinguishes valence intensity from arousal, allows for dominant and secondary affective states, and naturally accommodates mixed-valence configurations beyond a strictly bipolar description. Revisiting representative landscapes of the model, we show how neutral, uncertain, polarized, and mixed-valence regimes arise as a function of contextual sensory information, learned historical evaluation, and externally supplied information. We further show that the resulting valence-arousal relation provides a theoretical basis for the upper-open V-shaped organization discussed in the affect literature, while also opening a natural route toward a dynamical description of affect and emotions.

title: Rewiring of adult neural networks - learning from structural plasticity across multiple scales
summary: Synaptic connections are continuously formed and eliminated even in adult neuronal networks. This process - called structural plasticity - allows networks to change their topology to learn and adapt to their environment or compensate for lesions. Yet, in contrast to synaptic plasticity, structural plasticity is less well studied and understood. We here present the current state of knowledge as well as open problems in the field along three guiding questions: (1) What regulates structural plasticity in biological neural networks? (2) What are the functional consequences and advantages of structural plasticity in adult neural networks? (3) How can our understanding of structural plasticity be translated into clinical and technological applications? We argue that understanding structural plasticity is a problem involving multiple temporal and spatial scales. Solving this problem thus requires collaborative efforts of experimentalists, theoreticians as well as computational modelers, and has the potential for comprehensive neuroscientific insights that can guide the development of medical applications, artificial neural networks as well as neuromorphic computing.

title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
summary: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

title: Model-Based Cortisol Replacement Strategies for Patients With Adrenal Insufficiency
summary: Cortisol is an essential hormone secreted by the adrenal glands. Abnormally low level of cortisol is referred to as adrenal insufficiency. This paper focuses on devising treatment strategies for patients suffering from adrenal insufficiency using a model-based approach. Two conditions of adrenal insufficiency are analysed. They are hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) and adrenal gland disorders. The hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands constitute the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates stress and maintains physiological homeostasis through cortisol secretion. A comparative analysis of the existing mathematical models of the HPA axis is conducted. Based on this analysis, a novel model of the HPA axis is proposed that incorporates endogenous circadian rhythm. This proposed model is used to design effective cortisol replacement strategies. In addition, hydrocortisone replacement therapies are proposed and validated with clinical data from the literature. The results presented in this paper are applicable to patient-specific treatment strategies for individuals with adrenal insufficiency.

title: Physiology-Informed Sparse Identification of Dynamic Crop Models
summary: Developing resilient crops requires models that accurately capture how plant growth dynamics emerge from the continuous interplay between genetic and environmental factors. While high-throughput phenotyping platforms generate data for dynamic growth models, current modelling approaches show limitations: process-based crop growth models (CGMs) capture environmental dynamics but are difficult to scale across many genotypes because they require calibration of many parameters, while quantitative genetic models allow modelling many genotypes but often summarise time-varying environments using static covariates. To address this gap, we propose a data-driven framework to identify reduced systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describing crop growth dynamics as functions of environmental variables and a controllable number of genotype-specific coefficients (GSCs). Using the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method, we infer model structure directly from data via sparse regression on a physiologically informed library of candidate functions. title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
summary: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.

title: Probability generating functions for epidemiological time series
summary: Probability generating functions (PGFs) are a fundamental tool in mathematical epidemiology to characterize the stochastic evolution of epidemics via branching process theory. However, they are rarely used as operational tools in real-time during an outbreak, the main barrier being a lack of a systematic, computational methodology to describe epidemiological time series, such as cases or hospital admissions over time. Here, we introduce a general and computationally efficient framework for outbreak analytics based on PGFs. We first develop a method to encode joint distributions of incidences and their noisy measurements by realistic surveillance systems. Then, by transforming PGFs to cumulant generating functions (CGFs), we enable efficient evaluation of these joint distributions. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach for Bayesian inference and short-term forecasts, offering a significant computational advantage over simulation-based methods. Altogether, our framework operationalizes generating functions and paves the way for their broader adoption in computational epidemiology.

title: Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
summary: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

title: TetraCultures of Neurons, Astrocytes, Oligodendrocytes, and Microglia: A Murine In Vitro Model to Dissect Region-Specific CNS Immune Dynamics
summary: Neuroinflammation and glial scar formation in the central nervous system (CNS) emerge from coordinated signaling between neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia. Conventional embryonic neuron-astrocyte-oligodendrocyte (NAO) TriCultures lack microglia and cannot model innate immune responses. Here, we introduce postnatal neuron-astrocyte-oligodendrocyte-microglia (NAOM) TetraCultures, in which resident microglia are retained from the original brain tissue and co-develop with other CNS cell populations from the onset of culture. Hippocampal and cortical cultures were maintained for 14 days in vitro and challenged with LPS, poly I or scratch injury. Only NAOM TetraCultures mounted robust, region- and stimulus-specific inflammatory responses. LPS induced marked TNF-αand IL-1βsecretion and increased IBA1 in hippocampal microglia, whereas poly I elicited IFN-βrelease without increasing IBA1. CD68 regulation differed between hippocampus and cortex, and microglial morphology showed pronounced amoeboid transitions after LPS. Astrocytes in NAOM TetraCultures expanded their territorial coverage after LPS, an effect absent in NAO TriCultures. Following scratch injury, IL-1βincreased, microglia infiltrated lesion zones and astrocytes formed lesion borders. Thus, NAOM TetraCultures recapitulate key features of CNS immunity, glial scar formation and region-specific glial responses while providing a physiologically relevant microglia-containing model.

title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
summary: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.

title: SIGHT: A Methodological Appraisal Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated across ophthalmic tasks, yet the methodological quality of these evaluations has received little attention. Most studies report accuracy while overlooking design features required for valid and clinically meaningful inference. We critically reviewed published ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies covering knowledge assessment, patient education, diagnostic reasoning, triage, clinical documentation, multimodal image interpretation, and uncertainty estimation. We used the methodological weaknesses that recurred across study designs to develop the SIGHT framework, which has five domains: Sample and item provenance, Independence and blinding, Ground truth and comparator fairness, Handling of paired and repeated-measures data, and Transparency and trustworthiness. Current evaluations rely heavily on benchmark accuracy, synthetic clinical vignettes, and curated datasets, and real-world clinical validation remains rare. Common limitations include potential training-data contamination, inadequate handling of paired data, limited assessment of inter-rater reliability, inconsistent reference standards, insufficient evaluation of calibration and uncertainty, and frequent overinterpretation of benchmark performance as evidence of clinical readiness. SIGHT provides twenty structured appraisal items to evaluate internal validity, interpretability, and applicability across diverse ophthalmic LLM study designs. It offers a practical way to appraise ophthalmic LLM studies and may improve the methodological quality, interpretability, and clinical relevance of future evaluations.

title: A Robust Numerical Framework for Multi-Strain Epidemics
summary: Epidemiological models often take the form of systems of differential equations of varying levels of complexity. In multi-strain models, complexity arises from the interaction of diverse pathogen types that may exhibit different patterns of cross-immunity due to the host's immune system. Where previous work has tended to focus on theoretical analysis of this complexity, or model simplification, less effort has been given to efficient numerical exploration of full multi-strain disease dynamics. Here, we propose a computational framework for representing multi-strain disease transmission models, through a mathematically transparent hard-coded mapping between sets and integers. By mapping infection histories into Boolean matrices, the framework eliminates explicit iteration over strain combinations while preserving key biological processes, including sequential infection and partial cross-immunity. Benchmark comparisons of numerical solutions of our matrix formulation and a set-indexed implementation demonstrate substantial performance gains. Across models with increasing numbers of strains, the matrix formulation consistently reduces runtime, with a speedup exceeding two orders of magnitude for systems with 11 strains. We present an application of this approach to the case of COVID-19 in Indonesia, focusing on the replacement of the Delta variant by Omicron. We hope that our approach represents a robust computational approach to automatically generate diverse multi-strain epidemic models that can be solved in a computationally efficient manner for a variety of scientific and public-health questions.

title: Temporal invariance of evolutionary entropy and comparative demographic analysis
summary: Does evolutionary entropy depend on the width of the age classes used to describe a population? We show that the apparent dependence on temporal resolution is a consequence of the loss of information about reproductive timing within discrete classes. When this information is retained, corresponding continuous and discrete representations yield the same cycle entropy, generation time, evolutionary entropy, and reproductive potential in a common unit of time. When within-class timing is unknown, a uniform local reconstruction yields a logarithmic correction. For constant post-maturity hazard and fertility, continuous exponential and discrete geometric descriptions correspond exactly at every time scale. Thus, for a fixed reference duration, evolutionary entropy is a property of the reproductive process, not of its temporal partition. These results provide a mathematical basis for comparing demographic models across different temporal scales by identifying the information required to separate differences in reproductive organisation from effects of the chosen age-class representation.

title: Simple model of neurogliovascular unit activity with noradrenaline leading force
summary: In this work we present a model of a neuroglivascular unit associated with a neuronal ensemble. We combine calcium dynamics in the astrocyte, the cascade of synthesis of arachidonic acid and its derivatives, as well as the activity of the network of inhibitory and excitatory neurons with changes in local blood flow. We add equations to the model for extracellular neurotransmitters such as GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine. We show that the resulting model can exhibit different types of behavior, and also shows a significant connection between the functioning of the neural network and its supporting components.

title: Data-Driven Discovery of a Hyperelastic Strain-Energy Function for Veins Using Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Veins are commonly subjected to altered mechanical loading in clinical settings such as vein grafting, arteriovenous fistula creation, and tissue-engineered vascular graft implantation, making accurate constitutive models of venous tissue clinically important. Venous mechanical behavior differs characteristically from that of arteries, and existing constitutive models struggle to simultaneously fit the circumferential and axial stress-stretch responses across vein types. Here, we present a constitutive artificial neural network (CANN) framework that discovers a compact, interpretable hyperelastic constitutive model from biaxial mechanical data across three types of veins (saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava). The framework incorporates an expanded candidate function library with structurally motivated terms representing progressive fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions. Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation-based pruning, and response-level family collapse were then used to reduce the discovered basis to a compact strain-energy density function (SEF). The resulting eight-term SEF achieved significantly higher fitting accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three types of veins $(R^2>0.9, p<0.01)$. These findings establish a framework for constitutive model discovery in veins and propose a candidate constitutive form for further validation across larger, independent cohorts.

title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
summary: Is a chromosome a miniature of its genome, with the same mix of functional elements as the whole? We ask this of eight annotated genomes: human, mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize. Elements are classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements (TEs), pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) down to finer classes. Units are chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. We compare each unit with the genome and with other units, call compositions homogeneous when they differ by less than 5%, and score each against a random sample of the same size. The first finding is a surprising homogeneity. The level-1 compositions of the major chromosomes match each other and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast and C. elegans, and in fly down to the major arms. Finer classes can be homogeneous too: protein function in Arabidopsis, and the Wicker TE orders in maize. Enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable between chromosomes in all eight genomes. The second finding is a structured heterogeneity. Where a unit departs from its genome, it does so in one of three ways: clusters of named elements, such as rRNA genes or immune receptor loci; megabase-scale compartments, such as TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin; and lineage-specific gene families, visible only at the finest levels. Corrected for chance, the genomes fall into groups. For protein function and gene families, composition is more uniform in plants and fly than in vertebrates, and least uniform in C. elegans. For the major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows where each genome places its repeats, along the arms (maize, zebrafish) or around the centromeres (Arabidopsis, fly), not its lineage.

title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
summary: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.

title: Effective transport statistics for cooperative molecular motor ensembles with tether slack
summary: We improve upon our previous work using asymptotic analysis to characterize analytically the effective transport properties of a stochastic model for an ensemble of a cargo being pulled by two molecular motors walking on a microtubule. The governing equations are a system of stochastic differential equations with stochastic switching due to attachment and detachment kinetics of the molecular motors from the microtubule. Our model adopts a nonlinear tether which exerts no force when end-to-end distances are sufficiently small. This challenges some of the scale separation arguments from our previous work, and we modify the asymptotic analysis accordingly. In particular, spatial dynamics of the molecular motors may not always reach their quasi-stationary distribution within a particular attachment state. Rather, molecular motors tend to have a slack connection to the cargo for a while after they reattach, and we incorporate some first passage time analysis to determine if the tether becomes taut again. Through these and other modifications to the asymptotic analysis argument, the theoretical statistics for the run length, run time, and velocity of the motor-cargo ensemble can be brought into reasonable agreement with direct model simulations of two-motor ensembles consisting of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2. Additionally, we propose a new data fitting approach to obtain a double-exponential parameterization for the detachment rate of a motor as a function of the momentary force on its tether to the cargo, which is continuous at low load. Such a modified parameterization is needed to avoid artifacts in theoretical modeling of intracellular transport.

title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
summary: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

title: Ensemble-Based Modelling of Optogenetic Bioprocesses under Phototoxicity
summary: Optogenetics enables methanol-free protein production in the yeast $\textit{Komagataella phaffii}$ using light as a control input, facilitated by the blue-light-responsive transcription factor EL222. This opens the door to more programmable protein production in the food and biopharmaceutical industries. However, excessive illumination can inhibit growth and protein accumulation in some of these engineered cell factories. Previous hybrid modelling used black-box regression across sparsely sampled conditions to infer light-dependent kinetic parameters, without explicitly representing intracellular regulation. Here, we develop a multiscale mechanistic model linking EL222 activation, transcription, and translation to protein, biomass, and substrate dynamics. A latent light-associated stress state represents photoinhibitory effects on growth, transcription, and translation. An ensemble-based parameter-estimation strategy combines repeated global-local optimisation with screening for parameter sets supporting locally stable intracellular steady states under specified light conditions. Using available batch data for yeast-enhanced green fluorescent protein production in a $\textit{K. phaffii}$ strain carrying eight EL222 gene copies, the ensemble-mean predictions captured the main experimental trends in protein accumulation and growth across six constant light intensities. Parameter variability was propagated to time-course predictions, providing an empirical assessment of parameter-related uncertainty. Wider prediction bands coincided with less complete experimental coverage of the growth phases. Overall, the framework provides a mechanistic basis for future model-based optimisation and control of optogenetic bioprocesses under phototoxicity.

title: A mathematical model for fitness effects on viral persistence
summary: Persistent viral infections arise from complex interactions between viral replication, host cell responses, and ongoing viral evolution. A general framework linking viral fitness to persistence dynamics is lacking. Here, we develop for the first time a mathematical model of viral persistence that takes into consideration viral fitness variations. Essential to the model is the partition of the classical fitness parameter into three components: replicative, infective, and dispersal fitness. The model was initially inspired by a new experiment on hepatitis C virus (HCV) persistence, established in human hepatoma cells, also reported in this work. This experiment documents two strikingly different viral trajectories depending on the initial replicative fitness of the viral population used to establish persistence. The dynamical model describes the interactions among uninfected cells, infected cells, and infectious virions, and it incorporates, through a continuum, two alternative mechanisms of viral release from cells: budding and lysis. Analysis of the model reveals that viral fitness parameters organise infection outcomes into distinct dynamical regimes. Low replicative and dispersal fitness values lead to viral extinction, whereas high values enable persistence through either stable coexistence or recurrent infection waves. The space of fitness discloses a hierarchy among these parameters, with replicative and dispersal fitness being able to trigger important shifts in the outcome of the infection as opposed to infective fitness. The model identifies trade-offs between replication and dispersal that shape viral production and predicts slow dynamical regimes in which infection may persist despite low detectable viral loads. It provide candidates mechanisms capable of generating the persistence patterns observed experimentally.

title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
summary: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
summary: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.

title: Amortised Global Sensitivity Analysis of Pharmacokinetic models for Simulated Clinical Trials
summary: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models are used in simulated clinical trials to compare dosing protocols and patient groups before a trial is run. Distinct virtual patient cohorts, representing renal impairment, obesity and overdosage, can impose different input distributions on the same model. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) identifies which uncertain inputs drive the cohort's predictions, but a direct analysis incurs its full computational cost for every cohort. An alternative accounting is proposed here: a single surrogate is trained on an input envelope wide enough to contain every cohort, each cohort is then analysed using that surrogate, and the reported quantity is the number of cohorts at which the surrogate route has cost fewer mechanistic evaluations than the direct route. The study tests three GSA methods: variance-based GSA, Morris screening and optimal transport. It covers four PK and PK/PD models with seven to twenty-three free inputs, 21 cohorts and five surrogates. Every estimate is scored against a converged mechanistic solution obtained with its own method, and all costs are expressed in mechanistic model evaluations. The parameter ranking is recovered at low cost: gradient-boosted trees reconstruct it on 20 of the 21 cohorts and cost fewer evaluations to train than one direct cohort analysis, on all four models, at break-even counts between 0.02 and 0.14 cohorts. Amortisation is fastest at the highest dimensions, where each direct variance-based sample of a $D$-input model requires $D+2$ evaluations while the training budget does not scale accordingly. Recovering absolute index values is harder, and fewer surrogates manage it as inputs grow: two of the five surrogates fail at fifteen inputs, where the gradient-boosted trees and the Gaussian process still succeed, and at twenty-three inputs no surrogate succeeds on a majority of cohorts.

title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
summary: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $Δ=θ_E-θ_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $Δ=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $Δ\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

title: Association of Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin with Glycated Hemoglobin and Multidimensional Biomarker Structure in Reproductive-Age Women: An Analysis Based on NHANES 2021--2023
summary: Background: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is linked to adiposity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, but nationally representative evidence on the shape of the continuous SHBG-HbA1c association in reproductive-age women remains limited. Methods: We analyzed NHANES August 2021-August 2023 data for nonpregnant women aged 20-44 years (n=843). Survey-weighted linear regression related log-transformed SHBG to continuous HbA1c, with quadratic and spline tests for nonlinearity and tests for age modification. Forty biomarkers in hormone, biochemical, hematologic and inflammation/lipid blocks were analyzed by multiple factor analysis, sparse PLS and LASSO with bootstrap stability selection, with nested cross-validation. Results: After adjustment for age, race/ethnicity, poverty-income ratio and BMI, ln(SHBG) was inversely associated with HbA1c (beta=-0.1454, P=0.00083). Quadratic (P=0.00386) and spline (P=0.00236) tests supported nonlinearity, with a steeper slope at lower SHBG. The ln(SHBG)-by-age interaction was significant (P=0.0169). Adjustment for BMI, waist circumference and HOMA-IR attenuated the coefficient by 43.7%, 48.1% and about 55%. SHBG remained associated with HbA1c after conditioning on leading biomarker axes (beta=-0.1062, P=0.00342) and was selected in 98.8% of 500 LASSO bootstrap resamples. Nested cross-validation gave out-of-fold R^2 of 0.1298, 0.2136 and 0.2392 for clinical, biomarker and combined models. Conclusions: Higher SHBG was associated with lower HbA1c in a nonlinear pattern among reproductive-age women. The association overlapped with adiposity and insulin resistance but persisted after adjustment. The cross-sectional design and limited fasting subsample preclude causal or clinical interpretation.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Systems Biology Reconstruction of Diabetic Bone Marrow Dysfunction
summary: This study aimed to reconstruct a regulatory network suitable for systems biology analysis of diabetic bone marrow. Three artificial intelligence large language models independently analysed 18 Discovery and 43 Validation publications. Investigator guided integration produced a frozen network of 62 biological entities and 79 directed interactions. Open source software Gephi created a visual representation before and after main node removal. The plausibility of the reconstructed interactions was tested against independent curated knowledge resources, including the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, connectomeDB2025, Reactome, and Gene Ontology. Further analysis examined physiological correspondence, missing edge sensitivity, and graph constrained interrogation. Functional modules encompassed endothelial perivascular support, stem cell retention and trafficking, neural circadian regulation, inflammatory myelopoiesis, metabolic stress, and epigenetic regulation. They intersected through shared effects on endothelial function and stem cell behaviour. The endothelium was the principal connecting node. Computational removal of the endothelial node increased network fragmentation and diameter, while average directed path length remained essentially unchanged. External resources supported 60/79 interactions (75.9%); 19 remained unresolved, with none classified as contradictory. Complementary assessments supported biological plausibility and faithful interrogation of the reconstructed network. This investigator led dialogue with artificial intelligence provides a foundation for a systems level understanding of diabetic bone marrow dysfunction. The approach may facilitate the generation of testable hypotheses and the identification of mechanistic targets for coordinated restoration of disrupted niche interactions.

title: RetroTAC: Learning Route-Derived Synthetic Accessibility for PROTACs
summary: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) enable targeted protein degradation, expanding therapeutic opportunities beyond conventional inhibition. However, assembling their large, multifunctional structures creates synthetic challenges that hinder their discovery. Traditional synthetic-accessibility scores can overestimate this difficulty by penalizing PROTACs' molecular complexity while overlooking modular assembly from accessible building blocks. In contrast, retrosynthesis planning tools provide explicit routes but are computationally expensive, particularly for large molecules. Here, we introduce a human-interpretable, PROTAC-oriented route-derived score that rewards short synthetic depth and balanced joining of molecular fragments, and RetroTAC, a machine-learning surrogate that predicts this score directly from molecular structures. RetroTAC combines complementary models in an ensemble, achieving a root mean squared error of 0.13 and an $R^2$ of 0.65 on held-out molecules. We further evaluate its utility on PROTACs enumerated by recombining warheads, linkers, and E3-ligase ligands, followed by retrosynthetic planning and route analysis. Candidates selected for high predicted scores achieve a mean route-derived synthesizability of 0.73, compared with 0.31 for low-score candidates; 98.75% versus 51.00% are fully resolved under the tested search settings. These results support RetroTAC as a fast prioritization tool for virtual PROTAC libraries, connecting molecular screening with interpretable route characteristics while reserving explicit planning for selected candidates.

title: Leaky protection reveals three patterns in the relative advantages of vaccination strategies across transmission intensity
summary: Targeted vaccination often prioritizes individuals who contribute most to transmission. However, this rationale may change under leaky protection, whereby vaccination reduces susceptibility at each exposure rather than fully preventing infection. Here, we use a survey-derived individual-level exposure framework for 2,279 residents to simulate infection dynamics across ranges of transmission intensity and vaccine efficacy. We compare two vaccination strategies: the high-exposure strategy (prioritizing highly exposed individuals) and the oldest-first strategy (prioritizing older individuals). As transmission intensity changes, we identify three patterns in the relative advantages of these two strategies. At low transmission, the high-exposure strategy outperforms the oldest-first strategy in reducing both epidemic peak size and final infection proportion. At intermediate transmission, it lowers epidemic peak size but increases final infection proportion, revealing a trade-off between these metrics. At high transmission, differences between the strategies narrow, and the oldest-first strategy has a slight advantage for both metrics. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of considering vaccine failure mode when evaluating vaccination policies under different transmission dynamics.

title: EEG Entrainment to Non-Speech Rhythmic Patterns Associated with Dimensions of Language Performance
summary: Developmental dyslexia (DLX) affects 5-12% of the global population and impairs learning to read. Its biological basis, particularly the difficulties observed in oral phonological tasks, remains debated. Entrainment, the coupling of brain oscillations to speech rhythms, is essential for encoding phonological representations. We investigated whether brain entrainment to non-speech rhythms could predict DLX in 48 participants listening to white noise amplitude-modulated at rates matching Spanish speech units. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) signals yielded accurate DLX prediction for the 40 Hz stimulus using the Heights Ratio PAC measure (balanced accuracy 0.929, p = 0.0069, in the best case), indicating a stronger phonemic entrainment deficit in dyslexic individuals. Regression analysis in control (CTL) participants showed a strong dependence between reading performance scores and greater entrainment in language-associated brain regions. In particular, participants with poorer phonemic awareness, reading comprehension, or rapid automatized naming showed greater right-hemisphere entrainment to the 40 Hz stimulus. This finding adds evidence for the hemispheric compensatory mechanisms hypothesized in the literature. In conclusion, our methodology identifies dyslexia-specific entrainment patterns near language-associated brain regions, together with compensatory entrainment in right-hemisphere areas.

title: Physiology as Topology: Intervenable Organ Graphs for Longitudinal Patient Forecasting
summary: Do language models forecast patient trajectories by reasoning through physiology, or by fitting surface statistics? We introduce PhysioCircuit, a multi-agent agent system that represents each organ as an agent and each physiological relation as an editable mechanism card with direction, lag, and evidence. Its expert-defined graph is frozen at inference, enabling controlled edge interventions. We also introduce PhysioCircuit-Bench, a mechanism-controlled benchmark spanning three organ systems, treatment events, and real ICU admissions. We evaluate intervention-direction agreement (IDAR), which requires the affected organ to change in the expected direction within the expected lag window. The expert graph substantially outperforms all topology controls on edge-IDAR, including fully connected, random, and reversed graphs. Independent clinician adjudication supports the counterfactual results. PhysioCircuit transfers to new organ systems by configuration alone, without retraining, while preserving inspectable and editable relations.

title: Beyond Anxiety and Avoidance: A Dynamic Feedback-Regulation Framework for Adult Romantic Attachment
summary: Adult attachment is commonly represented by attachment anxiety and avoidance, but these person-level dimensions do not by themselves specify how momentary relational conditions are perceived, compared with desired conditions, translated into action, and updated after interpersonal feedback. We present the Attachment Regulation and Control (ARC) framework as an integrative feedback-regulation account that makes these temporal assumptions explicit and empirically testable. In ARC, control refers to feedback-based regulation toward relational goals in the control-theoretic sense, not interpersonal dominance, coercion, or a generalized need for control. ARC does not claim a novel control-system architecture. Instead, it synthesizes established control-theoretic attachment ideas, secure-base representations, perceived partner responsiveness, relational discrepancy, dyadic regulation, and recovery into a parsimonious sequence for adult romantic relationships: perceived relational state, desired relational state, discrepancy, regulatory action, partner feedback, state updating, and recovery. The framework treats the discrepancy score itself as a falsifiable modeling restriction by comparing it with perceived-state-only, unconstrained perceived-plus-desired-state, and asymmetric discrepancy alternatives. Attachment anxiety and avoidance form core regulation moderators. Secure-base representation is a candidate requiring incremental prediction of recovery outcomes. Mentalized affectivity and regulation flexibility remain optional moderators, while adult disorganization is an independent extension outcome.

title: Excitability across scales: a unifying EI model
summary: Neuronal excitability is commonly modeled using different principles at the cellular and population scales, making it difficult to study how microscopic mechanisms shape macroscopic activity. We introduce a spatiotemporal excitatory-inhibitory (EI) model that unifies these scales through a common mixed-feedback architecture. The model retains the conductance-based circuit structure of Hodgkin-Huxley models and describes intrinsic and synaptic currents through memductances whose temporal and spatial voltage dependence encodes dynamics at the relevant scale. In its minimal form, temporal excitability arises from fast excitatory feedback opposed by slower inhibitory feedback, while spatial excitability arises from short-range excitation opposed by longer-range inhibition, recovering the core lateral-inhibition motif of Amari neural fields. We show that combining these mechanisms gives rise to population excitability in strongly heterogeneous populations. In particular, the model generates population spikes that are localized in both space and time and possess population-level scales distinct from those of individual neuronal spikes, despite substantial cell-to-cell parameter variability. We then show that both intrinsic temporal excitability and spatial synaptic feedback are required for coherent mean-field events and robust spatiotemporal population rhythms. Finally, selective modulation of memductances in a subset of the population tunes the frequency of the population rhythm, illustrating how changes at the cellular scale can shape macroscopic dynamics. By separating circuit architecture from modeling scale, the proposed framework provides a physically interpretable approach to analyzing and designing neuronal excitability across scales.

We introduce a spatiotemporal excitatory-inhibitory (EI) model that unifies these scales through a common mixed-feedback architecture. The model retains the conductance-based circuit structure of Hodgkin-Huxley models and describes intrinsic and synaptic currents through memductances whose temporal and spatial voltage dependence encodes dynamics at the relevant scale. In its minimal form, temporal excitability arises from fast excitatory feedback opposed by slower inhibitory feedback, while spatial excitability arises from short-range excitation opposed by longer-range inhibition, recovering the core lateral-inhibition motif of Amari neural fields. We show that combining these mechanisms gives rise to population excitability in strongly heterogeneous populations. In particular, the model generates population spikes that are localized in both space and time and possess population-level scales distinct from those of individual neuronal spikes, despite substantial cell-to-cell parameter variability. We then show that both intrinsic temporal excitability and spatial synaptic feedback are required for coherent mean-field events and robust spatiotemporal population rhythms. Finally, selective modulation of memductances in a subset of the population tunes the frequency of the population rhythm, illustrating how changes at the cellular scale can shape macroscopic dynamics. By separating circuit architecture from modeling scale, the proposed framework provides a physically interpretable approach to analyzing and designing neuronal excitability across scales.

title: FlyHack: Stress-Testing Mechanistic Claims in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
summary: Connectome-constrained neural networks make biological components directly accessible to intervention, but their mechanistic conclusions can still depend on the comparison model, intervention, circuit representation and trained solution. We stress-test these dependencies in flyvis, a \emph{Drosophila} motion-vision model, using its 50-model ensemble, task-matched causal CNN controls and replicated interventions. At the level of model behaviour, three-level reverse-phi reversal in flyvis is strongly period- and velocity-dependent and also appears in task-matched CNNs; neither family reproduces the fly's stationary-sawtooth response. Adversarial direction reversal requires a perturbation bound of 0.21--0.27 times stimulus contrast in flyvis versus 0.13--0.25 in CNNs, but the gap over a parameter-matched CNN largely closes for larger CNNs. At the level of mechanism, matching attribution to the intervention matters: for held-out-mean replacement, first-order edge attribution patching reaches pooled AUROC 0.970 and Spearman 0.872, versus 0.933 and 0.126 when its zero-aligned score is evaluated against the same ground truth. Circuit conclusions also vary with representation and ensemble member. Greedy cell-type sets meet a model-relative T4/T5 tuning criterion in 25 of 50 models, while T4/T5 output silencing reduces the tested optic-flow behaviour to at most two of eight clips in 40. In six models where the cell-type search first succeeds, the corresponding connection sets can be pruned to 13--31 added classes; under an additional two-sided response-amplitude check, only two of those six first-success cell-type sets still meet the tuning threshold. These results support a narrower use of connectome-constrained models: they make mechanistic hypotheses directly testable, but the resulting claims must be scoped to the model family, intervention, representation and trained solution.

title: TopoLIA: Topology-Inspired Latent Interaction Attention for Drug Discovery
summary: The growing sophistication of drug discovery calls for new advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Transformers have underpinned recent breakthroughs in AI, yet their conventional source-target attention mechanism can become a bottleneck for modeling complex interactions. Here, we introduce TopoLIA, a topology-inspired latent interaction attention mechanism that learns not only how much information should be exchanged between interaction partners, but also how that information should be transformed. Source-target-dependent attention is mediated through a compact latent interaction space, providing a structured representation of complex interactions. We further incorporate topological spectral representations to capture multiscale data geometry and extract algebraic relationships. TopoLIA thus incorporates topological principles into both data representation and neural network architecture. We demonstrate TopoLIA on protein-ligand binding, where persistent spectra encode multiscale topological and geometric patterns in 3D protein-ligand complexes, while latent interaction attention (LIA) enables structured, source-target-dependent information exchange. We pretrain TopoLIA by reconstructing masked multiscale spectral tokens from unlabeled molecular structures, yielding transferable structural representations without task-specific annotations. Across multiple scoring and docking benchmarks, TopoLIA achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms its standard-attention counterpart. Rank analyses show that compact latent dimensions yield the best performance, supporting compact interaction spaces as an effective inductive bias for biomolecular learning. More broadly, LIA provides a general framework for structured, source-target-dependent information exchange that is applicable to diverse scientific and AI problems involving complex heterogeneous interactions.

title: Energy, Information, and the Limits of Neuropsychiatric Classification
summary: Importance: The search for reliable neuroimaging biomarkers of mental disorders has remained elusive despite decades of research. Why clinically consequential disorders yield weak neuroimaging separability remains unresolved. Drawing on statistical thermodynamics and the metabolic costs of neural coding, we propose that psychiatric disorders produce constrained deformations of a largely shared repertoire of brain activity patterns, limiting the class-specific information available for classification. Observations: We develop a framework linking physical resource constraints, landscape deformation, distributional separation, and attainable classification, and examine its components using human neuroimaging, synthetic data, and an exactly specified physical model. In resting-state fMRI from 1952 FOR2107 participants (823 with major depressive disorder; 1129 healthy controls), held-out energy-landscape estimates and nonlinear classifiers agreed across 13 comparisons (r = 0.996). Similar results emerged at both FOR2107 centers and in 900 SRPBS participants spanning multiple psychiatric diagnoses. In synthetic data, classification improved with distributional separation and approached the optimum. In an equilibrium three-well model, statistical energy equaled physical potential energy scaled by inverse temperature. Modest deformation redistributed state occupancy while optimal snapshot classification remained weak. A literature map found insufficiently comparable evidence to test the human metabolic constraint. Conclusions: Clinically consequential differences may arise within a largely shared neural repertoire. The thermodynamic framework connects physical deformation to classification under specified assumptions; its metabolic implementation in humans remains untested. Testing this mechanism requires joint measurements of brain activity, bodily physiology, and metabolism.

title: A minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction
summary: Rate-induced tipping ("R-tipping") in ecological modelling is characterised by too-rapid change of an environmental parameter causing collapse of a population without any bifurcation being crossed ("B-tipping"). A well-known example of a slow-fast predator-prey model in which R-tipping is observed [Vanselow, Wieczorek, Feudel, Journal of Theoretical Biology, 479, 64-72 (2019)] suffers from unecological "resurgence", whereby populations driven to functional extinction recover towards stable coexistence. We propose an analytically tractable model, incorporating a strong Allee effect into the prey dynamics in a slow-fast Lotka-Volterra-type predator-prey system, which induces bistability and thus renders the extinction state a genuine attractor. Applying geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT), we describe the dynamics of the extended model that is obtained by "ramping" of the inverse prey carrying capacity. We show the presence of a parabolic-shaped, folded critical manifold which admits a folded saddle singularity, the strong canard of which separates solutions that track the moving coexistence state from those that tip to extinction. The analytical simplicity of our model allows us to derive explicit expressions for the critical rate that separates "tracking" from "tipping" dynamics. Finally, we argue that our system represents a minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction, in that it incorporates three essential ingredients: bistability, a folded critical manifold, and a folded-saddle-type canard.

title: Unlocking the Regulatory Genome by ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Single Nucleotide Variants
summary: Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine. Large language models prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate transcription factor (TF) binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and assign biological significance to statistically negligible signals. We present ARGUS (Agentic Regulatory Genomics for an Uncertainty-aware Scientist), which strictly separates deterministic biological computation from LLM-mediated reasoning. ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop where a planner selects evidence sources based on current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path. On variant rs6983267 at the 8q24 cancer risk locus, the same planner produces four divergent trajectories for four TFs. FOXA1 is rescued in 3 steps when real ADASTRA allele-specific binding data (15 experiments, FDR = 0.030) reveals a model false negative masked by saturation. KLF6 traverses 8 steps across ADASTRA, JASPAR motif analysis, and ENCODE cCRE regulatory annotation before abstaining due to mixed indirect evidence. RAD21 abstains in 8 steps after ADASTRA returns a coverage-qualified but nonsignificant allelic test (5 experiments, FDR = 0.65), and SP1, which shares FOXA1's saturated retained prediction, abstains because no direct experimental evidence exists at this locus. All observations come from real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries; none are simulated. A comparison of fixed-priority and LLM-mediated planning shows that the LLM planner reaches identical verdicts with fewer tool calls by declining evidence that cannot resolve the claim under test.

title: La-Ribo: RNA Co-Design via Geometry-Latent Flow Matching
summary: RNA function arises from the coupling of nucleotide sequence and three-dimensional structure, motivating their joint design. Coordinating global folding with nucleotide-level detail remains challenging under limited structural supervision. We introduce La-Ribo, a generative framework for RNA sequence-structure co-design via geometry-latent flow matching. La-Ribo retains a sparse phosphate-sugar--base scaffold and encodes nucleotide identity and local conformation in residue-wise latents. A shared flow network generates both jointly, and an RNA-specific decoder then reconstructs all heavy atoms. To expand supervision, we construct a quality-controlled corpus of 168,561 RNA structures, integrating experimental data with predictions from three folding models, including 10,631 MSA-supported structures generated in this work. La-Ribo improves designability and codesignability over the evaluated baselines across sampling budgets and two refolding models, and the same prior supports scaffold-conditioned inverse folding without additional training.

title: Neural Decoding as Cognitive Inference
summary: The brain maintains stable cognition despite continuously changing neural activity. How to extract stable cognitive states from variable neural observations remains a central problem in neural decoding. Existing neural decoding methods map neural observations to predefined external labels based on the stimulus-response principle, often capturing recording-specific spurious correlations. Inspired by how the brain infers the world, and specifically by Bayesian brain theory, we recast neural decoding as cognitive inference constrained by brain-intrinsic priors, yielding high-level meta-neural semantic representations. In decoding experiments spanning five neural recording modalities and three cognitive domains (motor, perception and internal mentation), our cognitive inference method reorganized the geometry of neural observation representations, yielding meta-neural semantic representations that exhibited consistent geometric relationships across cognitive tasks and enabled the recovery of stable cognitive states from variable neural observations. Our work provides an account of how the brain maintains relatively stable cognition despite continual changes in the external environment. Cognitive stability is sustained through cognitive inference from changing neural activity, without requiring fixed neural activity patterns.

title: Elucidating the Space of Enzymatic Reaction: A Unified Benchmark and Pretrained Model
summary: Existing reaction models primarily learn molecular transformations, whereas enzy- matic reactions depend jointly on molecular structure and catalytic function. We formulate this problem as learning an enzymatic reaction space linking reactants, products, and Enzyme Commission (EC) annotations. To characterize this space, we introduce VenusRX-Bench, a unified benchmark for forward reaction prediction, single-step retrosynthesis, and EC-number prediction. VenusRX-Bench integrates reactions from multiple biochemical databases with standardized curation, leakage- controlled splits, and consistent evaluation. Benchmarking representative chemical and enzymatic models reveals a clear chemical-to-enzymatic domain gap, driven by limited domain data, catalytic-context dependency, and the difficulty of modeling large biomolecular structures. To bridge this gap, we develop VenusRX, a unified T5-style sequence-to-sequence model for enzymatic reactions. VenusRX jointly learns forward prediction, ret- rosynthesis, and reaction reconstruction, with two-stage training on millions of template-expanded reactions followed by real biochemical reactions. In addition, optional EC conditioning incorporates catalytic context, while Molecule Library- Constrained Decoding improves the generation of complex biomolecules. Across benchmark tasks and challenging generalization splits, VenusRX achieves the best or competitive performance on most evaluated settings over representative chem- ical and enzymatic baselines. Moreover, EC information consistently improves reaction prediction, while learned reaction representations support accurate EC prediction, revealing a bidirectional relationship between reaction structure and catalytic function. Together, VenusRX-Bench and VenusRX provide a unified framework for elucidating and modeling enzymatic reaction space

title: Cross-species representation learning aligns mouse and human neural dynamics and tracks clinical drug efficacy
summary: Preclinical models poorly predict human drug efficacy, particularly in neurological disorders. Neural activity offers a uniquely rich source of translational information because it captures high-dimensional variation in nervous-system function that can be measured in both animals and humans. However, its high dimensionality makes it difficult to distinguish conserved disease-related features from variation arising from species, recording modality and experimental context. Here, we test whether shared neural dynamics can be identified directly from electrophysiology data by learning representations organized by biological state rather than species. We develop a dual-rule contrastive learning framework that aligns corresponding mouse and human states while preserving separation between distinct phenotypes. This framework recovered conserved sensory-response structure across species and, in epilepsy, resolved distinct relationships between three mouse models and heterogeneous human patient populations. title: If the brain were so simple: Information-based drivers of intelligence and their interaction through an n-body-inspired framework
summary: Theories of how the brain processes information and returns intelligent outputs are numerous and often difficult to conclusively test. Here, we consider an approach grounded in informatics and algorithmic thermodynamics for how neural systems respond to different patterns of information in different ways, with a focus on the relationship between the information entropy of a signal and a new proposed quantity we term information enthalpy, which represents the internal resource of structured information within a system available to be used for predictions and other forms of work. To evaluate the capacity of the external signals to increase information enthalpy in the system, we introduce the information enthalpy potential (IEP) as a defined metric. We propose and implement a method for quantifying the amount of potential information enthalpy - the IEP - in a given signal across a range of example signals. We offer a conjecture of how information enthalpy may be treated by neural systems within a biological framework before showing how it may integrate and offer falsifiability to existing approaches such as the Free Energy Principle. This framework is also positioned in light of the role of neural criticality. Finally, we postulate a testable and falsifiable framework where the distinct mechanisms within each driver interact through a described n-body-inspired model to govern the "motion" of a neural system through a high dimensional state-space. Through these processes, it is proposed that these features form the most fundamental basis of the neural drivers that give rise to the complexity of adaptive behaviors that are commonly called: intelligence.

title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data
summary: Researchers often pool public gut microbiome datasets from immunotherapy studies to get around small sample sizes, assuming that adding cohorts adds statistical power faster than it adds differences between studies. We test that assumption. We processed four public shotgun metagenomic cohorts of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade through one pipeline and pooled them step by step, from 39 to 283 patients. Because the PERMANOVA effect size R^2 is above zero even when there is no real effect, we compared every result with its exact chance expectation. Measured as raw variance explained, cohort membership accounted for 8 to 27 times more variance than treatment response, although much of that ratio comes from sample size alone. At every pooling step, treatment response explained no more variance than chance (within 0.2 percentage points) and was never significant, while cohort membership explained 6.0 to 9.5 percentage points beyond chance (p = 0.001 each time). Classification stayed at chance across three model types, none of six leak-free batch-correction strategies recovered signal, and no genus reached significance in a random-effects meta-analysis. The largest single cohort (n = 165) was also non-significant, although simulation shows it had at least 90% power to detect an effect at its own 95% upper bound; within it, recruiting site alone explained 7.0 percentage points beyond chance. In three tumor genomic cohorts (n = 223), a small but real response effect sat next to a cohort effect about eighteen times larger, so the problem is not specific to microbiome data. We release batch_detector, an open tool that reports chance-corrected cohort and response effects before pooling, and test it on an independent colorectal cancer meta-analysis.

title: Mean Field Theory Based on the Spike Time Response Curve for Synchronization Within and Between Two Alternating Populations of Neural Oscillators with Delays
summary: In order to study oscillators coupled by pulses emitted at discrete times, it is generally assumed that the effect of each pulse is an instantaneous phase shift, with a possible conduction delay between emission and receipt. However, we are interested in neural oscillators in which each pulse (action potential) activates a biexponential synapse, and at high frequencies, the duration of the synaptic conductance may be greater than the network period. Therefore, the effect of received pulses can summate over the course of several cycles. To overcome this limitation, we previously defined a mean field approach for a single synchronous population. Here, we extend it to two alternating synchronous populations by assuming a perturbation of a single oscillator from one of the synchronous populations which is represented by a single self-connected neural oscillator. The train of delayed biexponential synapses emitted by each oscillator is divided into a tonic and a phasic component. Because of the continuous rather than pulsatile nature of the input, we had to drop the concept of oscillator phase and derive self-consistent criteria for the existence and stability of an alternating firing pattern between two synchronous populations based solely on the perturbation of time intervals from their steady state values. Simulations showed that for high frequency oscillations as defined above, the mean field approach predicts the existence and stability of phase-locking between two synchronous populations better than the instantaneous phase shift approach. This approach may generalize to other forms of coupling amongst non-neural oscillators.

title: The Role of Tick Questing Behavior and Host-Finding Success in Borrelia burgdorferi Transmission in the Eastern United States
summary: The marked difference in reported human Lyme disease cases between the northeastern and southeastern United States remains a significant concern. Differences in biodiversity and the questing behavior of Ixodes scapularis, the primary vector of Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, have been proposed as key drivers of geographic variation in disease incidence. In this study, we investigate how these differences, together with ratio-dependent tick-host contact rates, contribute to the north-south gap in Lyme disease cases. Building on our previous work, we develop a discrete-time system of difference equations to model infection dynamics between ticks and their sylvatic hosts. We derive an expression for the basic reproductive number and vary key parameters to assess their impact on infection persistence. We further examine the effects of these mechanisms on nymphal infection prevalence (NIP) and the density of infected nymphs (DIN), two key metrics for predicting disease risk. Our results indicate that under baseline conditions, southern host communities exhibit lower infection prevalence and reduced potential for pathogen invasion, consistent with observed regional patterns. However, southern host communities can support sustained transmission with different questing behaviors. Notably, this qualitative north-south difference emerges using parameter values obtained from the literature, without calibrating the model to reproduce geographic differences in disease prevalence. In addition, ratio-dependent host-finding success shows a saturating effect on the basic reproductive number, compared to the traditional assumption of density-independent host-finding success. These results highlight the importance of biodiversity, tick questing behavior, and using multiple metrics when assessing Lyme disease risk.
