title: Magnetic shocks generated by two counterstreaming plasma jets induced by an intense femtosecond laser pulse
summary: This work extends the investigation of magnetic control of counterstreaming laser-produced plasma jets reported in Zemskov et al. (2026), focusing on the experiments performed in the presence of a uniform 14 T magnetic field oriented transverse to the jet propagation. When generating plasma flows using 60-80 fs, 10-15 J pulses at the PEARL facility, we observe the formation of narrow, stationary layers with strong magnetic-field amplification and sharp plasma-density gradients in the interaction region. We interpret these features as the result of compressing the externally applied transverse field by the converging plasma ram pressure. The external magnetic field is advected and compressed until its magnetic pressure balances the decreasing ram pressure of the jets. Time-resolved interferometry, shadowgraphy, and Faraday polarimetry, combined with hybrid PIC--fluid simulations, reproduce the formation of a high-field barrier that decelerates and laterally redirects plasma flows while producing multiple density jumps. We discuss the astrophysical implications: the compression of an initially weak ambient field by converging flows provides an efficient, non-turbulent channel for magnetic-field amplification that can render interstellar magnetic fields dynamically important - a condition essential for diffusive shock acceleration in supernova remnants. Our experiments therefore establish a laboratory platform bridging externally magnetized and self-magnetized regimes and offer a complementary route to magnetic-field amplification in high-energy astrophysical shocks.

title: Optimization of curved vortex generator geometry for enhanced thermal performance in water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger
summary: In the study, the geometry of curved rectangular vortex generators (RVG) has been optimized to enhance heat transfer and overall performance of the analyzed water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger (FTHE). The developed and validated conjugate numerical model includes a small section of the full-scale heat exchanger representing the computational domain, with fully developed velocity and temperature profiles specified at the inlet boundaries of the water. Four influential geometry parameters of the vortex generator were selected for the optimization; attack angle, curvature angle, axial position in the streamwise direction and height. The optimization process has been performed according to two criteria: maximization of heat transfer solely and maximization of heat transfer while considering the influence of pressure drop. Accordingly, one objective function related to the Colburn factor (j) and two objective functions combining the Colburn factor and the friction factor (f) were defined. The regression analysis has been used and the Central composite design of experiment was selected in order to obtain non-linear regression polynomial functions which were integrated into the investigated objectives. The optimization procedure has been performed using the genetic algorithm. Optimized configurations performance improvement was evaluated through comparison with the performance of the reference FTHE with plain fins. For the RVG configuration optimized according to the objective of maximizing heat transfer, the Colburn factor was enhanced by 53.1%. Optimizing the RVG configuration to maximize heat transfer while accounting for the influence of pressure drop resulted in an enhancement of the FTHE area goodness factor by 14.4% for one set of geometry parameters, and an enhancement of volume goodness factor by 26.5% for another.

title: Inferring cell property distributions from high-throughput measurement data with cell-to-cell variability
summary: High-throughput measurements of cell populations produce broad distributions of observables due to inherent cell-to-cell variability. While these distributions contain valuable biological information, extracting the underlying distributions of cellular properties remains challenging. We introduce the likelihood functional, a statistical framework that infers cell property distributions by combining experimental data with deterministic computational models. The method first evaluates the model on a discrete parameter grid. Optimization of the likelihood functional is then possible without repeated model evaluations and yields best-fit property distributions which enable the direct prediction of observable distributions for comparison with experiments. As a demonstration, we apply the framework to real-time deformability cytometry data and infer cytosol and membrane viscosity distributions of human red blood cells.

title: Neutron spectrometry of (p,n) based neutron fields at the University of Helsinki using the NCT-WES single-moderator directional spectrometer
summary: A tunable-energy neutron beam produced with up to 1 $μ$A / 10 MeV proton beam on a solid LiF target is available at the Department of Physics of the University of Helsinki for neutron metrology and research applications. This work presents the experimental characterisation of the neutron beams produced at the Helsinki Accelerator Laboratory, and the validation of the \texttt{MCNP6} and \texttt{GEANT4} radiation transport codes for simulating these neutron beams. The neutron spectra produced in the forward direction from 1960, 2040, and 2310 keV protons were measured using the NCT-WES single-moderator directional spectrometer. NCT-WES (Neutron Capture Therapy Wide Energy Spectrometer) is a recently developed single-moderator neutron spectrometer with a sharply directional response, and it is a very convenient instrument to characterise neutron facilities, as it determines the whole spectrum in a single exposure, and has a low sensitivity to room-scattering. The neutron fluence was also determined with the Berthold LB 6411 neutron monitor. The data acquired with NCT-WES were unfolded using the FRUIT unfolding code, starting from guess spectra obtained from \texttt{GEANT4} or \texttt{MCNP6} simulations. The unfolding analysis showed that both transport codes produced plausible spectra, \texttt{MCNP6} being more accurate for the 1960 and 2040 keV irradiations and \texttt{GEANT4} for 2310 keV. The measured values of energy-integrated neutron fluence agree satisfactorily with simulations as well as preliminary measurements with the LB 6411 neutron monitor.

title: Non-Markovian quantum-emitter dynamics and bound-state formation in an Aubry--André--Harper photonic lattice
summary: In non-Markovian light-matter interactions, a spectrally structured bath can alter the evolution of a quantum emitter by modifying the vacuum fluctuations experienced by the emitter. This raises the question of how the localization transition and the associated multifractal critical modes induced by a quasiperiodic potential shape the emitter dynamics. We investigate this scenario in the single-excitation sector for a two-level quantum emitter coupled to an Aubry-André-Harper (AAH) photonic lattice. By externally tuning the strength of the quasiperiodic onsite modulation, the lattice is tuned from the extended to the localized regime through a critical point characterized by multifractal modes. Using modal analysis, we show that the quasiperiodic modulation reshapes the local density of states at the coupling site and thereby controls the effective spectral coupling between the emitter and the lattice. The transient dynamics depend strongly on the spatial and spectral overlap between the emitter and the lattice modes: extended modes below the critical modulation generally produce rapid depopulation, whereas critical and localized modes give rise to coherent back-action and persistent Rabi-like oscillations, with particularly pronounced behavior at the critical point. We further identify emitter-photon bound states whose formation is controlled by the quasiperiodic spectral structure of the bath and whose overlap with the initially excited state leads to partial long-time population trapping. These results establish a direct connection between quasiperiodic localization, non-Markovian dynamics, and emitter-photon bound-state formation.

title: A flexible electronics and DAQ system for the Timepix4 ASIC
summary: The INFN Data Acquisition system (IDAQ) is designed for data-driven readout of the Timepix4 ASIC, supporting simultaneous time-of-arrival and time-over-threshold measurements with nanosecond precision. The system architecture combines dedicated hardware for high-speed serial data transmission, FPGA-based data processing, and a Trigger Logic Unit for synchronization and timing distribution. It operates in continuous streaming and triggered modes, ensuring low-latency and high-throughput performance. The system has been deployed in test-beam campaigns within the 4DPHOTON project, demonstrating stable operation, precise timing alignment, and reliable data handling under high-rate conditions.

title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
summary: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

title: From Airspace Degradation to Deconfliction: Predicting Safety-Critical Traffic States through the Evolution of Multiscale Complexity Metrics
summary: Growing air traffic demand is pushing airspace management towards the limits of its operational capacity, with steadily increasing workload for air traffic control officers, with direct consequences for safety. Understanding which traffic conditions give rise to safety-critical situations is therefore an essential open problem. Here we compare a large number of deconfliction events with equivalent conflict-free scenarios, extracted from thirteen weeks of air traffic control data over the Swedish Flight Information Region. We describe the traffic structure before each event through thirty sector-complexity metrics computed at multiple spatial and temporal scales, and use them as inputs of Machine Learning models. We find that the need of deconflictions can be predicted with an accuracy reaching $70\%$, but only when the traffic is described at the sector spatial scale. Predictability increases monotonically in the minutes preceding the clearance, showing that situations requiring deconflicting actions are not sudden occurrences, but rather the endpoint of a progressive degradation process. Additionally, the information needed for such prediction mainly resides in specific characteristics of the overall traffic structure, and not only in the conflicting pair. These results numerically demonstrate that safety-critical airspace states can be anticipated from the collective behaviour of the traffic, paving the way for early-warning systems that flag degraded, safety-relevant conditions before an intervention is required.

title: The Diffuse Layer of Thin Cylinders: Beyond the Counterion Condensation Paradigm
summary: For over half a century, the counterion condensation theory has served as the dominant view for highly charged cylinders, prescribing a sharp charge renormalization based on the idealized abstraction of a salt-free line charge. In this work, we resolve this problem for physical open-domain systems across all charge regimes using the method of matched asymptotics applied to the non-linear Poisson--Boltzmann equation with added salt. For subcritical fields, where the dimensionless charge parameter satisfies $ξ< 1$, cylindrical curvature suppresses non-linear coupling, leaving the diffuse atmosphere unmodified. Beyond the critical threshold ($ξ= 1$), where the linear theory breaks down due to a localized Boltzmann explosion, the counterion accumulation smoothly transitions into a local flat-wall near-field geometry. By matching these zones, we construct a unified, parameter-free composite analytical solution capturing the spatial crossover toward the global cylindrical Debye screening tail. In the supercritical regime ($ξ> 1$), this near-field regularization locks the far-field effective charge into distinct, concentration-dependent parallel plateaus. Crucially, within the realistic regime where $ξ\le 5$, these idealized plateaus are not always reached, and the effective charge operates within a smooth, variable transition zone. Throughout all regimes, the ionic atmosphere remains diffuse, proving that the limiting laws of condensation emerge as artifacts of omitting the screening electrolyte.

title: Evaluation of attenuation-based simulated X-ray images for image-guided radiotherapy
summary: In image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT), in-room X-rays are often used for patient positioning and monitoring, however, usually default imaging settings are utilized for each indication. Obtaining patient-specific imaging settings before treatment is achievable using simulated X-rays, which can facilitate IGRT workflow optimization. This study evaluated the image quality of simulated X-rays for thoracic, cranial and pelvic regions. Simulated X-rays were created from computed tomography (CT) scans with indication-specific default settings using a pre-release pilot software, which mimics the geometry of the room-mounted ExacTrac Dynamic (ETD) system (Brainlab SE, Germany). The basis of this algorithm was the Beer-Lambert law. Linear attenuation coefficients were approximated from the CT hounsfield units, while incident intensities were defined by flood images. CT scans were included from three anthropomorphic phantoms and 57 patients (13 lung, 20 glioblastoma, 24 prostate). For evaluation, real X-rays were used as ground truth. Three image quality metrics - Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC), Normalized Mean Absolute Error (NMAE) - complemented by histogram and intensity profile comparisons were used for evaluation. SSIMs for phantom and patient average were 0.87 and 0.80 for the thoracic, 0.94 and 0.88 for the cranial and 0.85 and 0.79 for the pelvic region. Corresponding NCCs yielded values of 0.99 and 0.89, 0.99 and 0.99 and 0.99 and 0.60. NMAEs were 4.1% and 10.7% (lung), 2.6% and 3.2% (brain) and 2.6% and 4.0% (pelvis). Histograms of real X-rays and simulated X-rays (sX-rays) were slightly shifted and showed differences at the background pixel value. Intensity profiles exhibited similar trends with some differences in absolute values. The investigated simulated X-rays demonstrated promising quality for individualized IGRT treatment preparation.

title: On the rise of a Taylor bubble-drop assembly in a vertical tube
summary: In a liquid-filled vertical tube, a Taylor drop typically rises far more slowly than a Taylor bubble owing to the much larger density and dynamic viscosity of the former. In this work, we demonstrate experimentally and numerically that instead of being slowed down by the attached drop, a Taylor bubble-drop assembly rises at the same velocity as an isolated Taylor bubble, leading to a significantly faster rise of the Taylor drop. We discuss the underlying mechanism and use an analytical model to predict the drop radius within the assembly. This phenomenon offers a means for bubble-assisted rapid transport of an immiscible liquid phase in vertical tubes, with potential applicability in gas-lifting systems in confined environments.

title: Symmetry-governed nonlinear metasurface simultaneously enhances circular dichroism, helicity purity, and Q-factor
summary: Circularly polarized light underpins a broad range of chiroptical and spin-selective photonic technologies, yet extending resonant chirality to nonlinear harmonic emission remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a symmetry-governed mechanism that maps the maximal linear chirality of high-Q degenerate resonances onto the polarization of the generated harmonic. Preserved rotational symmetry protects modal degeneracy and polarization-selection rules, while broken mirror symmetries enable a strong chiroptical response. The metasurface thereby filters the pump polarization and purifies the handedness of the nonlinear output, simultaneously achieving third-harmonic circular dichroism of -0.98, a degree of circular polarization of 0.83, and an effective nonlinear Q-factor of 140. Importantly, the nonlinear emission preserves its handedness even under spatially depolarized excitation, demonstrating robustness to variations in the incident polarization state. These results establish complementary symmetry preservation and breaking as a deterministic route for transferring resonant chirality from linear to nonlinear optical responses, providing a general design principle for nonlinear chiral photonics.

title: Near-Field Engineering of Silica-Shelled Plasmonic Nanoparticles toward Enhanced Near-Infrared Fluorescence
summary: Near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent molecules often suffer from low quantum yields, limiting their applications in sensing and imaging. Their fluorescence can be enhanced by coupling with plasmonic nanoparticles exhibiting resonances in the same spectral region. However, this approach requires precise nanoscale control over the plasmonic near-field. Here, we combine scanning transmission electron microscopy with electron energy-loss spectroscopy (STEM-EELS) and boundary element electromagnetic simulations to engineer silica-coated anisotropic plasmonic nanoparticles. We synthesised three types of nanoparticles, gold nanorods (AuNRs), gold bipyramids (AuBPs), and silver nanorods (AgNRs) with tunable NIR plasmonic resonances. Silica serves as a dielectric spacer, enabling precise control over the distance between the nanoparticle surface and a potential molecular emitter. To assess their suitability for fluorophore attachment, we investigated the dependence of the electric near-field on silica shell thickness. High-resolution STEM-EELS mapping revealed that thin silica shells (4.4 nm for AuNRs and 3.1 nm for AuBPs) allow most of the near-field to extend beyond the dielectric layer. For AgNRs, a thicker shell of 7.0 nm was required to prevent oxidation while maintaining near-field accessibility. Electromagnetic simulations further evaluated the optimal shell thickness and the dependence of fluorescence enhancement on particle geometry, material, fluorophore internal quantum yield, and fluorophore-metal separation. Together, these results provide practical design guidelines for optimizing particle morphology and sub-10 nm silica shells in plasmonic nanostructures for fluorescence enhancement.

title: Causality-informed dynamic mode decomposition for unsteady flow analysis
summary: Causal analysis characterizes directional dependencies in dynamical systems, while such information is not typically used to inform reduced-order modeling of unsteady flows. This study proposes a Granger Causality-informed Dynamic Mode Decomposition (GC-DMD) framework that incorporates such information into data-driven modeling and modal analysis of high-dimensional flow data. The framework uses conditional Granger causality estimates to regularize the identification of the DMD operator, preferentially suppressing weakly supported interactions while preserving dynamically relevant couplings. This regularization promotes sparse operators informed by directional predictive dependencies, leading to improved predictive accuracy and identification of dynamically relevant modes. GC-DMD is evaluated on a linear system with a known coupling structure, lid-driven cavity flows with varying dynamical complexity, and a broadband transonic turbulent jet. Compared with standard DMD, GC-DMD improves operator identification accuracy in the linear benchmark and improves the robustness of the identified spectrum while reducing long-horizon prediction errors in the cavity flows. For the turbulent jet, it yields a sparser operator with improved prediction accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of incorporating causality information to guide the identification of sparse, predictive reduced-order models of complex flows. title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
summary: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

title: Label-free Monitoring of Nucleoid Dynamics of Bacteria for Drug Screening Using Holography
summary: We introduce holographic microscopy (HM) as a compact, low-cost, label-free, non-specific alternative to fluorescence microscopy (FM) for quantifying bacterial physiological responses during drug screening. Using the regularized inverse holographic volumetric reconstruction (RIHVR) framework, we extract phase maps from HM images and then invert the reconstructed phase to generate fluorescence-like contrast, in which bright inverted-phase regions correspond to bacterial nucleoid content captured by FM signals. We show that this relationship holds across multiple bacterial species, growth stages, drug treatments, and post-treatment time points, demonstrating that HM can consistently capture nucleoid associated structural information without fluorescent labeling. Because HM phase images contain both whole-cell refractive-index information and internal nucleoid-associated contrast, they enable simultaneous quantification of cell boundaries, cell length, nucleoid size, and nucleoid occupancy. These measurements allow drug-induced changes in bacterial morphology and nucleoid organization to be monitored over time. Unlike FM, which can suffer from photobleaching and may perturb live cells through phototoxicity, HM relies on refractive-index variations and maintains stable signal quality for long-term live-cell imaging. By linking label-free phase imaging to nucleoid-scale physiological readouts, this work establishes a path toward automated, high-throughput, and experimentally simpler bacterial drug-screening assays.

title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
summary: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. title: Advance identification of where the 2026 Kumamoto earthquake would begin
summary: Long-term forecasts say how likely a fault segment is to rupture, not where the rupture will begin. The b-value, the slope of the earthquake size distribution, falls as stress rises. After the 2016 Kumamoto sequence in Japan, b-values rose along the ruptured faults but fell in the unruptured central part of the Hinagu fault zone, which we identified in 2019 as where the next rupture was most likely to begin. The 2026 M7.1 Kumamoto earthquake began at the edge of this area, inside the low-b-value volume at 16 km depth. To our knowledge, this is the first starting point of a large earthquake named in print beforehand. The rupture stopped at a fault bend where b-values have stayed low since 2000 and raised Coulomb stress on faults beyond it; the low-b-value zone at this bend is where the next rupture is most likely to begin.

title: Nonlinear dynamics of short-wave instabilities in a helical vortex within and beyond the weakly nonlinear regime
summary: The nonlinear evolution of a helical vortex with axial flow disturbed by an elliptic or curvature instability mode is investigated by direct numerical simulations. The normalized vortex core radius and reduced pitch are systematically varied to examine a wide range of linear growth rates, revealing two types of nonlinear evolution. At relatively small growth rates, both instabilities exhibit weakly nonlinear saturation, with the vortex and unstable mode structures largely preserved. Together with previous findings for other vortex configurations, these results reveal that weakly nonlinear saturation is a generic feature of short-wave instabilities. At larger growth rates, the instabilities reach higher energy levels and evolve beyond the weakly nonlinear regime, with the vortex and unstable mode structures substantially deformed. Comparison with weakly nonlinear analysis suggests that larger linear growth rates require larger disturbance amplitudes for nonlinear effects to balance linear growth. At these larger amplitudes, higher-order nonlinear effects and modal components not retained in the weakly nonlinear analysis become increasingly important, as demonstrated by the numerical results. This provides a new physical interpretation of the departure from the weakly nonlinear regime. Since helical vortices serve as a model for tip vortices shed from rotating blades, these results offer useful insights for tip-vortex control in wind turbines, which can potentially accelerate wake recovery and thereby improve turbine performance.

title: Linear-Stability-Guided Two-Stage Surrogate Model for Nonlinear ITG-TEM Turbulence
summary: We develop a two-stage surrogate model framework to predict the linear and nonlinear properties of ITG-TEM turbulence from GENE gyrokinetic simulations. The first stage uses a hierarchical ensemble of stability and mode classifiers, along with global and mode-specific regressors, to predict the linear growth rate and real frequency. The second stage uses these predictions as linear spectra in a Fourier neural operator (FNO)-based nonlinear surrogate model. The nonlinear model predicts saturated potential and heat flux spectra, together with zonal flow quantities. Two linear drive scalars, the maximum and integral of the linear growth rate over a low-wavenumber range, are also supplied directly to the networks predicting scalar quantities. For the architecture studied here, comparisons with models omitting either or both input paths show that linear information can improve spectral and scalar predictions under extrapolation toward stronger linear drive.

title: Magma Buoyancy Couples Lunar Mantle Convection and Magmatism: Long-Lasting Mare Volcanism and Radius Change in a 3-D Regional Model
summary: To understand the mantle evolution that has caused the observed histories of mare volcanism and radius change of the Moon, we developed a 3-D regional spherical shell mantle convection model with magmatism. Magma generated by decompression melting segregates from the convecting matrix and percolates upward through it. In our model, internal heating forms a basal partially molten layer during the first several hundred million years. Finger-like magma ascents then grow from the top of this layer and evolve into buoyant, partially molten plumes. The plumes ascend by the buoyancy of magma, while decompression melting in the ascending plumes generates more magma that further drives the ascent. Magma supply to the top of the mantle peaks between 4 and 3.5 Gyr ago, coincident with a maximum in radial expansion driven by volume change of the mantle associated with melting, and both decline as the mantle cools and solidifies. Magma supply, however, persists for billions of years because earlier plumes leave thermally softened conduits, through which later plumes repeatedly rise at fixed locations. These stable conduits are a consequence of the 3-D geometry. Recycling of magmatic products formed in the uppermost mantle also triggers renewed magma ascent through the conduits. Our results provide a mechanism for the observed long-lasting localized volcanism that peaked at 4-3.5 Gyr ago and quantitatively account for early expansion followed by contraction. The conditions required for consistency with the observed history imply an initially hot but mostly solid mantle with a dense basal layer.

title: P^2-Gaussian: Prior-Driven and Projection-Guided Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Cone-Beam CT Reconstruction
summary: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) reconstruction reduces imaging dose and scan time, but severe angular undersampling makes the inverse problem highly ill-posed. Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods initialize Gaussian primitives from Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructions that are contaminated by streak artifacts. The limited angular coverage also leaves the Gaussian parameters underconstrained, producing needle-like artifacts. We propose P2-Gaussian, a prior-driven and projection-guided 3DGS framework. In this framework, a latent rectified flow model, Sparse2Prior, first restores the artifact-corrupted FDK volume into an anatomical prior in approximately 5 s. Gaussian primitives are then initialized from this prior in a tissue-adaptive manner, which yields a compact representation with 62%-65% fewer optimized primitives than random sampling. During optimization, virtual projections synthesized at intermediate angles between the measured projections are activated in rotation, while measured projections remain dominant in the objective function. Experiments on 5, 10 and 20 measured views showed that the proposed P2-Gaussian achieved the highest PSNR and SSIM among all methods. Compared with the optimization-based Gaussian baseline, our method increases PSNR by 5.98, 4.25 and 2.49 dB and accelerates reconstruction by 2.6-3.0 times. These results indicate that coupling a learned anatomical prior with measurement-constrained Gaussian optimization is effective for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Ballbo5354/P-2-Gaussian.

title: Transition to turbulence in swirl created by a vertical magnetic field in liquid metal electrodes
summary: Flow transitions in electromagnetically-driven swirl in a cylindrical domain are investigated using three-dimensional simulations for a liquid metal battery electrode. The parameter space considered: applied current $I=11.11-100A$; Current density, $J_0 \approx 4,000-35,000 A/m^2$, domain radius, $R=3-9cm$, domain height, $H=3$ and $4.5cm$). The background magnetic field, $B_0$, strength is varied systematically from 0.1 to 20 G to characterize the route to chaos. \cite{davidson2022swirling} found the onset of chaos occurs around $1-1.5 G$ for aspect ratio $1/6$ and current of 100A, however, this is shifted to $16-17 G$ for a lower current of 16A and aspect ratio $1/2$. Across a range of geometrical configurations and forcing conditions, including variations in aspect ratio, current and current density, a consistent sequence of dynamical transitions is evident from phase portraits, FFT spectrum, 0-1 chaos test, autocorrelation function and correlation dimension. The flow evolution is by the Ruelle--Takens-Newhouse route to chaos, with the strange non-chaotic attractor (SNA) regime providing an intermediate state prior to the onset of chaos. In our results, it is observed that, for a fixed aspect ratio, the transition is governed by a dimensionless group, $Q_m$, representing the ratio of applied Lorentz force to viscous force. The critical value of $Q_m$ at the onset of oscillatory flow is found to be nearly invariant except when the domain height is varied. Moreover, our results follow the $Re \sim Q_m^{2/3}$ scaling law expected from torque balance moderately-forced electro-magnetically driven swirl flows.

title: Focal-Plane Extreme Adaptive Optics for Deep Super Resolution Imaging and Nanolithography
summary: Super resolution optical imaging and nanolithography enable nanoscale observation and fabrication, but high order, spatially varying phase and amplitude aberrations in optically heterogeneous media severely limit their performance at depth. Here we introduce focal-plane extreme adaptive optics (FP-ExAO), which moves beyond conventional phase conjugate correction by directly sensing and controlling the focal-plane complex field. This terminal field captures aberrations accumulated throughout the optical system. A state space formulation directly links deformable mirror commands to the focal field, avoiding explicit plane by plane Fourier optics modelling, while information theoretically optimal probing and closed-form control enable rapid field estimation and correction. Cascaded deformable mirrors further enable FP-ExAO to correct coupled phase-amplitude and spatially varying aberrations. In three-dimensional (3D) single molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), FP-ExAO enables imaging to 160 um depth in brain tissue and beyond 60 um in kidney tissue, while maintaining approximately 18 nm localization precision across a 75 um x 75 um corrected field, with a 16-fold larger field of view and more than tenfold faster correction than conventional AO methods. These capabilities meet the imaging requirements for 3D deep tissue optical connectome reconstruction and quantitative super resolution pathology. In stimulated emission depletion (STED) nanolithography, FP-ExAO reduces the minimum written linewidth from 251.1 nm without correction to 88.8 nm at a depth of 160 um in photoresist. FP-ExAO establishes a new adaptive optics paradigm for deep nanoscale optical readout and writing.

title: Position- and Temperature-Dependent Responsivity in a KID-Based Phonon-Mediated Detector
summary: We report on the position- and temperature-dependent response of a kinetic inductance phonon-mediated (KIPM) detector. To study position-dependence, we used a controllable mirror attached to a micro-electromechanical system (MEMS) to steer optical light with a 100 $μ$m spot size over the backside of the cryogenic detector. With both pulsed and continuous operation of the LED, we observe features of the detector housing and find that the signal is strongest when the LED is pointed directly at the KID. The "off-KID" response is measured to be 34% of the "on-KID" response and is largely independent of direction. We model phonon propagation and collection in the KIPM detector with G4CMP and assert that the isotropic angular dependence is unlikely to be due to discrete phonon absorption "sinks", such as the microwave feedline or the device mounting points, but can be explained instead by an isotropic energy loss in the crystal. We furthermore utilize the temperature flexibility of the MEMS and KIPM detector system to investigate temperature-dependent responsivity, both at the sensor level (i.e., frequency shifts in the KID) and at the detector level (i.e., position dependence). We fit the KID's response to a two-component heat capacity and present the model as an alternative way to understand the KID's response to absorbed energy. We show on- and off-KID data at a range of temperatures and show that the phonon dynamics are not temperature dependent. We comment on the resulting implication for KID dynamics and design improvements.

title: SD3: The First Operationally-Proven, Fully Heterogeneous-Accelerated Global Kilometer-Scale Model with Inline Physics Architecture
summary: We present Super Dynamics on the Cube (SD3), the first operationally-proven, fully heterogeneous-accelerated global kilometer-scale model. Through a full-stack reconstruction in native CUDA C, SD3 introduces an "Inline Physics" architecture that deeply couples its non-hydrostatic cubed-sphere dynamical core with fast physical processes. This design maintains high physical consistency, ensures energy and mass conservation, and mitigates "Grey Zone" mismatches. Five years of continuous operational forecasting, together with validation against diverse observations, demonstrates the scientific fidelity of SD3. Recently, SD3 achieved an unprecedented 205.7 simulated days per day at global 1.5 km resolution using 24576 GPUs. SD3 establishes a hardware-agnostic, portable, and reproducible paradigm across diverse Exascale ecosystems. Beyond weather and climate research, SD3 offers a transformative paradigm for the HPC community and the next-generation Digital Twin Earth to establish a robust, high-performance blueprint for the future of Earth system modeling.

title: Development of a Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Transition State Search in Molecular Systems: A Transferable Model Across Structural and Dimensional Variations
summary: We developed a DRL approach for TS searches combining the deep Q-network and the bidirectional long short-term memory architectures to handle variable-sized molecular systems. We applied our method to 1,3,5-hexatriene (Triene), alanine dipeptide (Ala2), and 1,3,5,7-octatetraene (Tetraene) as target systems with the search space limited to backbone dihedral angles. Our model successfully learned the TS search tasks for all examined systems. More importantly, we demonstrate that our model pre-trained on Triene exhibits distinct transfer-learning capabilities across both backbone modifications (Triene to Ala2) and chain extensions (Triene to Tetraene). Such transferability is highly promising for future applications to molecules in general, as it allows an agent trained on simple systems to accelerate TS searches in larger or more complex ones. We expect that these findings on cross-system transferability represent an important step forward in developing DRL-based approaches for TS searches.

title: Common Offset Gathers for Efficient Multistatic Beamforming in Frequency Domain
summary: Frequency-domain beamformers reconstruct ultrasound images with far fewer operations than delay-and-sum (DAS). However, for multistatic synthetic aperture data, they require Fourier transforms over the full transmit-receive aperture and large amounts of memory, limiting their use for volumetric imaging. Here, we adapt common offset gathers (COG) from seismic imaging to frequency-domain beamforming: transmit-receive pairs with the same offset are beamformed independently using a bistatic formulation, holding only one offset gather in memory at a time. We combine COG with the range-Doppler algorithm (RDA) and evaluate COG RDA against DAS and conventional multistatic RDA using simulated, phantom, and in vivo acquisitions. For linear arrays, COG RDA reduced memory requirements by two orders of magnitude relative to conventional RDA and beamformed up to 25x faster than DAS, with comparable image quality. For a 32x32-element matrix array, COG RDA requires only 2-D instead of 4-D Fourier transforms, and reconstructed a volume on a GPU 32x faster and with 67x less energy than DAS. COG RDA makes frequency-domain multistatic beamforming practical for matrix arrays and power-constrained devices.

title: Spatial-Mode Selection for Local Mineral Absorption Spectroscopy
summary: Absorption-band depth measures the fractional decrease in mineral reflectance below its local continuum. Recovering this feature strength for a small mineral region supports quantitative comparisons between regions, but diffraction mixes its light with the surroundings. Conventional spectral fitting can separate mean contributions; it cannot remove background photon noise already recorded. We develop a quantum-inspired measurement framework that uses spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) to retain the target absorption response while reducing background acceptance before detection. The framework connects finite mineral-region geometry and reference spectra to estimation precision. A loss-dependent design condition identifies when adding SPADE exposure improves on direct imaging (DI) under fixed-response Poisson measurements with unknown scene parameters. Joint inference from initial DI observations and both mode ports estimates target depth together with an unknown, spatially shared background spectrum. In equal-time simulations that include localization uncertainty, alignment time, calibration, and detector costs, this acquisition reduces depth root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 14\%--26\% across five absorption strengths relative to all-pixel DI with the same background freedom. These results use a supplied target feature shape and geometry, with target continuum slope fitted and curvature fixed. The analysis separates optical selectivity from parameter ambiguity and acquisition cost, providing a quantitative basis for spatial-mode receiver design in local mineral spectroscopy.

title: Generalized Discrete Fractal Dimensions of Graph Families
summary: Quantifying the self-similarity of complex networks via discrete fractal dimensions is a fundamental problem in network science. In this paper, we investigate some general fractal dimensions of graph families based on q-energy and Rényi entropy. We first establish several bounds for the energy, and then discuss the monotonicity, measure invariance of the dimensions, as well as some concrete graph families.

title: LesionStudio: A Patient-Informed Platform for Task-Specific Optimization of Emission Tomography Reconstructions
summary: Purpose: For task-specific PET and SPECT reconstruction optimization, we developed LesionStudio, an open-source platform incorporating patient background heterogeneity, realistic lesion morphology and texture, and lesion-background interactions beyond conventional phantoms. Methods: LesionStudio, a Python framework built on PyTomography, inserts lesions into PET/SPECT data using modality-specific forward projection and stochastic background ablation. Clinical realism was evaluated by physician review of 30 inserted lesions in eight DLBCL patients from a 1,579-lesion FDG lymphoma library. Quantification and detectability were assessed in FDG PET using spherical and patient-derived lesions varying in size, LBR, and site, reconstructed with OSEM and BSREM. Results: Inserted lesions were visually indistinguishable from true disease (AUC = 0.49). OSEM improved the patient-derived quantification limit from ~3.7 mL at iteration 4 to ~2.0 mL at iteration 10, but with increased noise and edge artifacts. Weakly regularized BSREM (beta = 5) achieved a similar ~2.0 mL limit with stability, whereas stronger regularization increased under-recovery. Detectability was contrast-dependent: no lesions were detected at LBR 2:1, whereas detectable volume ranged from 0.70 to 3.63 mL at LBR 4:1 and decreased to 0.70 mL at LBR 6:1-8:1 for both OSEM and weakly regularized BSREM. Conclusion: Reconstruction settings can shift SUV metrics and detectability enough to affect interpretation, so no single protocol suits every task. OSEM required early stopping for detection and feature stability but more iterations for mean-SUV quantification, whereas weakly regularized BSREM matched both at one setting. LesionStudio (https://github.com/qurit/LesionStudio), with our public library of realistic lesions, provides a reproducible framework for task-specific optimization across radiopharmaceuticals and scanners.

title: A Geometry-Induced Finite Warburg element for Reversible Diffusion Impedance at Microdisk Electrodes
summary: A compact analytical representation is developed for the diffusion impedance of a disk electrode under reversible conditions, obtained by transforming the chronoamperometric relaxation function into the frequency domain. A Padé approximant is constructed for the uniform-concentration boundary condition, preserving the finite low-frequency diffusion resistance of the steady-state disk current and the high-frequency Cottrell regime. It is extended to reactions in which both oxidized and reduced species contribute, with unequal diffusion coefficients and surface concentrations. Its accuracy is quantified against converged numerical solutions, including an exact solution of the coupled problem with finite-rate kinetics. The approximant reproduces the Saito resistance and the $45^{\circ}$ Warburg phase exactly; its modulus is within 0.6\% of the converged solution for $ωa^2/D\le12$ and 7\% below the Cottrell amplitude at high frequency. The uniform-concentration and uniform-flux boundary conditions both give a diffusion impedance of geometric origin, but differ by up to 11\% in modulus because each couples differently to the spreading diffusion field; a criterion based on the rate constant and the disk radius delineates where each applies. The exact solution shows that this crossover is broad and that the decomposition into a charge-transfer resistance and a diffusion impedance is accurate to about 5\% for $1\le2k^0a/D\le100$. Fitted to a published spectrum of a platinum microdisk, it reproduces the reported diffusion coefficient within 1\%, while the two limiting elements lie 4.8\% below and 4.1\% above it. The element is a practical tool for microdisk impedance analysis.

title: Nonreciprocal coupling enables tunable exceptional-point response in non-Hermitian circuits
summary: Exceptional points (EPs) exhibit characteristic square-root spectral responses to weak perturbations, with response magnitudes governed by configuration-dependent prefactors that are often relatively small. Modulating these prefactor while preserving the exceptional characteristics offers an additional degrees of freedom for engineering non-Hermitian sensing responses. Here, we report a nonreciprocal non-Hermitian circuit system with gyrator-meditated coupling that supports a continuous family of EP configurations. Unlike reciprocal coupling, which typically yields a unique EP configuration for balanced gain and loss, nonreciprocal coupling allows the directional forward and backward coupling strengths to be varied while maintaining their product and thus preserving the EP condition and yielding a library of EPs. This additional freedom enables continuous control of the frequency-splitting magnitude without modifying the square-root characteristic dependence on absolute perturbation strength. We show that the spectral splitting induced by a given absolute resistance perturbation can be enhanced by appropriately adjusting the coupling asymmetry. Theoretical predictions, circuit simulations, and experimental reflection-spectrum measurements consistently confirms this tunable response. Our results establish nonreciprocal coupling as an alternative approach for engineering and enhancing EP-induced perturbative responses without changing their characteristic branch-point scaling.

title: Numerical analysis of geometrical effect on drop deformation and breakup between rotating cylinders
summary: This study numerically investigates the effects of geometrical curvature on drop deformation and breakup in shear flow between counter-rotating concentric cylinders. Simulations were performed using a geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) method incorporating plicRDF interface reconstruction and isoAdvector interface advection, combined with adaptive mesh refinement. Three circular geometries with different values of the non-dimensional geometrical curvature, $κ_{\mathrm F}$, were considered and compared with a planar shear flow system. At fixed Reynolds and Capillary numbers ($Re$ and $Ca$), the breakup morphology differed substantially between the planar and circular systems. In the planar system, the drop underwent relatively symmetric neck thinning, whereas in the circular systems, the drop exhibited asymmetric deformation and pronounced azimuthal elongation. At higher curvature, the drop formed a thin filament that subsequently fragmented, producing multiple satellite drops. Analysis of the internal velocity field and the magnitude of the rate-of-deformation tensor revealed distinct flow and deformation structures associated with these breakup behaviors. Furthermore, the critical $Re$ for breakup, $Re_{\mathrm{cr}}$, decreased with increasing $κ_{\mathrm F}$ at nvestigated $Ca$ values. In contrast, the maximum dimensionless elongation length immediately before breakup at $Re=Re_{\mathrm{cr}}$ increased with $κ_{\mathrm F}$. These findings suggest that geometrical curvature affects not only the breakup threshold but also the deformation process leading to breakup, providing insights into drop breakup in curved shear flows.

title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls
summary: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate supersonic turbulent boundary layers subjected to continuous concave and convex surface curvatures. Scale-resolved spectral turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budgets, triadic energy-transfer bispectra, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), and global resolvent analysis are employed to elucidate the effects of compressibility and pressure gradients, and to distinguish the linear and nonlinear mechanisms at play. Over concave walls, the destabilizing curvature enhances pressure-strain redistribution, shifting near-wall turbulence toward a two-component state, and induces a shear-driven outer-layer production peak at low spanwise wavenumbers. Bispectral and SPOD analyses reveal that this outer-layer energy feeds a structured, multi-step triadic transfer toward fundamental large-scale and spanwise-uniform modes, which physically manifests as streamwise vortex breakdown rather than a three-dimensional inverse cascade. Global resolvent analysis further demonstrates that while nonlinear triadic interactions select the dominant scale amplitudes, the spatial topology of these coherent structures is dictated by linear mean-flow receptivity and spatially developing convective instabilities. Conversely, over convex walls, stabilizing curvature and dilatation attenuate pressure fluctuations and suppress pressure-strain redistribution, breaking the near-wall turbulent cycle and trapping energy within elongated, one-component streamwise streaks, while a localized resolvent wavemaker energizes the downstream recovery region.

title: Volumetric Nanophotonics for Enhanced Scintillation and Remote Light Outcoupling
summary: Nanophotonic patterning is a promising approach to enhancing light extraction in scintillator materials, with the potential to improve performance in applications such as medical imaging and particle detection. While 2D surface patterns have been successful in improving scintillator performance, the true potential of nanophotonic patterning lies in the bulk, where photons are emitted, transported, and absorbed. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the enhancement and control of scintillation using 2.5D volumetric nanophotonic patterns. title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
summary: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

title: Quantitative Ultrasound Perfusion Biomarker: Cross-Modality Validation with Laser Speckle Imaging
summary: Rationale and Objectives: Tooth extraction can cause alveolar bone resorption and variable healing despite socket preservation. Current perfusion assessment relies largely on visual evaluation, limiting objective monitoring of socket healing. We developed and validated a quantitative color flow ultrasound framework to reduce sensitivity to imaging settings and motion artifacts. Materials and Methods: Color flow ultrasound data were acquired longitudinally in 30 patients undergoing tooth extraction and grafting. Velocity- and power-weighted color pixel density (CPDvel and CPDpwr) were derived from complex-valued color flow (TRI) data at 0-1.5 mm beneath the epithelial surface. Gain robustness was assessed using a Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance (QIBA) flow phantom. Concurrent laser speckle contrast imaging (LASCA) provided in vivo comparison. Results: Phantom velocity estimates remained stable across color gain settings of 20-100 a.u. at flow rates of 2, 4, 6, and 8 mL/s. Perfusion metrics decreased over approximately 2-30 weeks after extraction. Nonlinear fits yielded R2 values of 0.74 for CPDvel, 0.45 for CPDpwr, and 0.66 for LASCA. Exponential half-decay times were 60.3, 92.4, and 48.3 days, respectively, relative to the first post-extraction measurement. LASCA correlated linearly with ultrasound-derived velocity (R2 = 0.68) and power (R2 = 0.74; both p < 0.05). Conclusions: The framework supports noninvasive, quantitative monitoring of superficial perfusion during socket healing with reduced sensitivity to color gain. Direct analysis of TRI data provides depth-specific perfusion metrics and may improve consistency across imaging sessions. Further validation is needed to determine its ability to identify compromised healing and inform clinical decisions.

title: From Dye to Dynamics: Quantitative Measurements of Fluid Flows from Vortex Geometry
summary: Although vorticity and passive tracers (such as dye) are both transported by fluid flows, there are subtle differences in how this transport happens. This indicates that dye cannot be used to track vortex motion in experiments, even though it has often been used for this purpose. In this manuscript we show that under proper circumstances dye can be used to accurately track the center-lines of vortex filaments. Moreover, we show that a number of important fluid quantities, such as energy and helicity, can be computed in terms of the shape of the vortex center-line. As a result, dye-tracked vortices are a valuable tool for measuring the properties of fluid motion in a variety of experimental situations. Moreover, we discuss techniques by which could be used to extract more detailed vortex information in future work.

title: 800 $^\circ$C Air-Ambient Operation of Extreme-Bandgap Al$_{x}$Ga$_{1-x}$N (x>0.6) Digital and Random-Alloy Channel HEMTs
summary: This work demonstrates the high-temperature (room to 800 $^\circ$C) operation of thin Al$_{0.62}$Ga$_{0.38}$N digital alloy (DA) short-period superlattice (SPSL), and random alloy (RA) Al$_{0.64}$Ga$_{0.36}$N channel MOSHEMTs on sapphire. The RA devices employ a doped $n^{+}$-85%-Al barrier and a highly doped $n^{++}$-Al$_{0.86\rightarrow0.20}$Ga$_{0.14\rightarrow0.80}$N reverse-graded layer (RGL) for surface ohmic contact formation, whereas the DA devices employ a binary AlN barrier and selectively regrown $n^{++}$-GaN source/drain contacts. At 800 $^\circ$C, the DA channel devices exhibit better thermal stability: their saturated drain current decreases from 460 to 172 mA/mm (62.6%) compared with 338 to 98 mA/mm (71.0%) for the RA channel, and a lower subthreshold swing (459 for DA versus 550 mV/dec for RA). All tested DA devices also exhibit superior threshold-voltage stability ($<\pm 10\%$ versus $>\pm 19\%$ for RA) and maintain an ON/OFF current ratio >$10^4$ at 800 $^\circ$C, compared with ~$10^3$ for RA, thus establishing the DA channel HEMTs as a promising new platform for high-temperature electronics.

title: A 3D measurement workflow for assessing replication quality and tool degradation in moulded microfluidic channels
summary: Mould-based replication, such as injection moulding with 3D-printed inserts, needs a check of how faithfully microchannels are transferred from master to polymer replica. It is usually limited to a width or depth ratio from one cross-section, which misses the sidewall shape and depends on where the section is taken. We present a workflow that assesses the whole channel from 3D scans of master and replica, without sectioning. The scans are registered on a common grid, and each height map is converted into a map of local slope. The correlation of the two slope maps over the channel interior, RQ$_d$, is reported with the channel dimensions and height- and slope-error maps. These outputs separate a change of shape from a change of size and locate it. A user can thereby compare mould materials, detect tool wear, and tell whether a deviation arose before or during moulding. On synthetic channels with known degradation, RQ$_d$ fell steadily as the sidewalls were rounded, whereas the height correlation levelled off. For injection moulding with stereolithography-printed inserts in three resins, RQ$_d$ ranged from 0.17 to 0.91 over fifteen insert-to-part pairs. The height correlation placed the ten well-formed channels within 0.03. Over a twenty-shot run, one insert's RQ$_d$ fell from 0.90 to 0.72 as its sidewalls wore, while its height correlation stayed above 0.93. We developed open-source software that implements the workflow. Because the workflow needs only registered 3D scans of a master and its replica, it can in principle be applied to other mould-based processes.

title: Simulating scintillation detector responses with OpenMC and pyMPPost: a track-based coupling verified against MCNPX-PoliMi
summary: Simulations of the detector response are essential for the design and analysis of neutron and photon measurements in nuclear nonproliferation, safeguards, and active interrogation studies. MCNPX-PoliMi, combined with the post-processor MPPost and its Python implementation pyMPPost, is a well-established and validated framework for this purpose. Its detector models, however, are not available to users of the open-source Monte Carlo code OpenMC, which does not write an equivalent collision-level output. This work couples OpenMC to pyMPPost, allowing the open-source community to use the detector models already implemented and validated in pyMPPost without modifying either code. A Python class, $\texttt{TrackAnalyzer}$, reads the particle tracks written by OpenMC, reconstructs the interactions in the detector material along with the target nuclide and writes them in the MCNPX-PoliMi collision file format. The method relies only on the track output and is therefore applicable to any OpenMC version that writes particle tracks, including the development branch with photonuclear physics used in this work. The coupling was verified code to code against MCNPX-PoliMi for a trans-stilbene and a $^{4}$He scintillator exposed to $^{252}$Cf and deuterium-deuterium fusion neutron sources, and for a NaI(Tl) scintillator exposed to $^{137}$Cs and $^{152}$Eu photon sources. The total number of pulses agrees within $\pm$1\% in all cases, and the light-output spectra agree within a few percent in the covered spectral domain. By making the detector response models of pyMPPost available within a fully open-source simulation chain, this work extends detector response studies with OpenMC to nuclear nonproliferation and active interrogation applications, including those involving photonuclear reactions, and provides an accessible tool for education and training in radiation detection.

title: Molecular Electrodynamic Relaxation in Dielectric and Plasmonic Cavities
summary: Molecular radiative emission is a fundamental relaxation process that governs excited-state lifetimes and significantly influences photophysical dynamics, but direct self-consistent Maxwell--Schrödinger simulations of molecular radiation suffer from numerical instabilities in evaluating radiative self-interaction. Herein, this issue is resolved within the self-consistent propagation of classical Maxwell's equations coupled to real-time density-functional electronic dynamics and their tight-binding approximation. By carefully removing the longitudinal components of radiative self-reaction, this framework quantitatively reproduces radiative lifetimes of atomic and molecular emitters in vacuum and further captures cavity-modified emission at weak and strong coupling regimes beyond perturbation theory. For molecules weakly coupled to an optical microcavity, the cavity Purcell effect is shown to reach maximum using a modestly red-detuned cavity due to nuclear thermal motion. Moreover, for a single methylene blue molecule strongly coupled to a realistic nanoparticle-on-mirror plasmonic cavity, the predicted molecular electrodynamical relaxation is accelerated to approximately 11 femtoseconds, directly competing with nonadiabatic nuclear dynamics. This work establishes a route to first-principles design of material radiative properties in a wide range of dielectric environments.

title: Simulation-Derived Angular Migration in Volcanic Muography
summary: Transmission muography usually treats each angular bin as a straight line of sight through the target. Multiple Coulomb scattering can break this mapping by changing the muon direction in rock. We introduce CABRIALES, a reduced model that represents this effect as migration between source and destination angular bins. The input muons are generated with a conditional normalizing flow trained on ARTI simulations, selected with a continuous-slowing-down range threshold, and deflected using angular distributions derived from Geant4. We apply the model to four observation points at Cerro Machin volcano in Colombia. Among the muons selected by the transmission threshold, 41.4-45.1% move to a different 2.5-degree bin within the field of view, while 20.7-24.3% reach a different rock-intersecting angular bin associated with a longer rock path in the terrain model. For muons with energies within 5% above the transmission threshold, the changed-bin fraction increases to 67.4-81.3%. Destination maps further show that events arriving from shorter assigned paths can form a large share of the modeled population in some rock-intersecting bins. These results quantify angular redistribution before detector response; they do not represent net count changes or density bias.

title: Theoretical Study of Classical Dynamics of Electron in Two-Frequency Paul Trap
summary: We present a theoretical study of trapping an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap, motivated by future hybrid architecture consisting of a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca$^{2+}$) and an electron. By isolating the electron from ionic-electron interactions, we formulate the equations of motion for the electron in the time-dependent trap potentials and cast them in the Hill form. Stability and dynamics are then analysed in terms of the dimensionless q-parameters, which encode the applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and the particle's charge-to-mass ratio. Under the combined action of the two radio-frequency fields, the trapped electron's classical motion is shown to be approximated well by a slow secular oscillation modulated by two distinct motion sidebands originating from the low- and high-frequency RF drives. The approximation method presented here enables a quick evaluation of the relation between the device-design q-parameters and the electron motion. It offers a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.

title: High-Repetition-Rate Laser-Driven Fast Neutron Generation from Planar Liquid Heavy Water Jets
summary: We demonstrate a high-repetition-rate, directional pitcher-catcher neutron source employing a continuously flowing, ambient-temperature liquid jet pitcher and a beryllium catcher target. title: The impact of an in-situ stress gradient on the growth of a fluid-driven frictional rupture
summary: Models of injection-induced aseismic slip commonly assume uniform in-situ stresses along the fault, and thus predict rupture growth symmetric about the injection point. We relax this assumption and account for linear variations with depth of the resolved shear and effective normal tractions. We consider a planar fault with constant friction under plane-strain conditions, subjected to fluid injection at constant overpressure. Vanishing stress intensity factors at both rupture tips yield two coupled equations for the up-dip and down-dip tip positions. We solve them semi-analytically and compare the results with numerical simulations. The stress gradient notably breaks the self-similarity of the uniform-stress solution. Growth is then governed by two parameters. The first is the fault-stress injection parameter $\mathcal{T}$, ratio between the initial distance to failure at the injection point and the effect of the fluid overpressure. The second is the ratio of the diffusion length $\sqrt{4αt}$ to a stress-gradient length scale $L_c$, namely the initial distance to failure at the injection point divided by its gradient along the fault. Growth is symmetric at early times. In the marginally pressurized regime, rupture lags behind the pressure front and the relative asymmetry grows as $1.1\,(4αt/L_c^2)^{1/2}$. The up-dip tip then accelerates markedly compared to the down-dip tip. In the critically stressed regime, rupture outpaces diffusion by a factor of order $1/\mathcal{T}$, and the relative asymmetry grows as $\sim 0.34\,(4αt/\mathcal{T}^2L_c^2)^{1/2}$. The up-dip tip reaches $\sim L_c$ earlier, and the ratio of up-dip to down-dip rupture lengths remains below two.

title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
summary: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.

title: Local neoclassical calculations using a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space basis with advanced collision operators
summary: We present radially local neoclassical (NC) calculations based on a Hermite-Laguerre (HL) velocity-space polynomial expansion combined with advanced linearized collision operators, including the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau (FPL) operator. The implementation is verified against the NC code SFINCS using both a multi-species Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like (LBD) operator and the FPL operator, the NC fluxes agreeing to within 3% in the Pfirsch-Schlüter regime. The accuracy of the HL basis is then assessed by convergence studies against the Legendre-Laguerre (LG) basis. At an equal number of spectral coefficients, neither basis is uniformly more accurate. In the plateau regime, the LG basis is more accurate on the particle and heat fluxes, which are sensitive to the trapped-passing boundary, whereas the HL basis is more accurate on the bootstrap current, carried by the parallel flow. In the banana regime, both bases converge slowly. Finally, we compare the LBD and the original (OS) and improved Sugama (IS) operators against the FPL operator. The IS operator retrieves the NC fluxes to within 6% over four decades of collisionality, whereas the LBD operator overestimates the ion heat flux by a factor of 2.6 to 4.7. The OS operator overestimates the ion heat flux by 4 to 33%, while retrieving the particle flux and the bootstrap current to within 9% and 18%, respectively. The convention adopted for the LBD collision frequency also changes the bootstrap current by up to two orders of magnitude. The present work extends the use of the HL basis, previously used in turbulent calculations, to NC physics and, to the knowledge of the author, these are the first NC calculations using the HL basis.

title: Mitigating Errors in Variational Quantum Eigensolver Calculations through Extended Random Phase Approximation
summary: Quantum hardware noise remains a major obstacle to accurate molecular simulations using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We introduce a novel error-mitigation strategy based on the extended random phase approximation (ERPA), which reconstructs the two-particle reduced density matrix (2-RDM) from approximate transition density matrices, effectively filtering errors in quantum measurements. Unlike quantum subspace expansion, the approach requires only the one- and two-particle RDMs. Since ERPA preserves the input 1-RDM, we further propose a hybrid quantum-classical scheme employing an inexpensive density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculation to provide a noise-free approximation to this quantity. Benchmarks on water double-bond stretching and cyclobutadiene automerization, performed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrate reductions in energy errors by orders of magnitude. Combined with multireference adiabatic connection (AC0) corrections, the approach additionally recovers dynamical correlation beyond the active space, yielding accurate molecular potential energy curves and reaction barriers. Our results establish ERPA as a promising, measurement-efficient route toward reliable quantum-classical electronic structure calculations.

title: Options for heating, fueling, and current drive in MANTA, a high-field negative triangularity fusion pilot plant
summary: In this work, we assess how the performance of MANTA, a high-field, highly radiative, negative triangularity tokamak concept, depends on pellet fueling, ion cyclotron resonant frequency (ICRF) heating, and lower hybrid current drive (LHCD) schemes. Negative triangularity (NT) has been gaining momentum in the fusion community as a naturally, robustly ELM-free regime that is capable of power plant level performance. The MANTA device has been the subject of previous works regarding the whole-device design, power handling and divertor assessments, and core transport optimizations. Informed by these previous studies, we assess whether changes to the original MANTA heating and current drive scheme can positively affect performance, both in terms of lowering scrape-off layer power (improving power-handling, a primary benefit of NT) and maximizing plasma gain to levels necessary for an attractive fusion pilot plant. In this work, we find that the MANTA concept can yield improved performance in terms of plasma gain and scrape-off layer power by simultaneously going to lower input power and higher seeded impurity fraction. Also, we find that increasing the fueling magnitude can increase fusion power while minimally impacting scrape-off layer power. Performance can also be improved by optimizing the ICRF design; decreasing the minority ion fraction, decreasing the toroidal mode number of the injected wave, and switching from a helium-3 minority ion to a hydrogen-1 minority ion all result in increases to fusion power. The additional inboard space afforded by the NT geometry provides an opportunity for wave launch to be moved to the inboard side. This is beneficial for LHCD access and results in a wide range of potential current profiles in the edge, with the total driven current due to 25 MW of LHCD reaching up to 1.2 MA, or about 12% of the total current.

title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
summary: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

title: The Ensemble Ghost Interaction in Fractional-Occupation Hartree-Fock: Occupation Covariance, Pair Rank, and Prescribed Ensembles of Determinants
summary: Fractional Occupation Number unrestricted Hartree-Fock (FON-UHF) evaluates the UHF functional on a density matrix with non-integer occupations. Sector-Averaged UHF (SA-UHF) averages the energies of a prescribed ensemble of determinants, possibly from different particle-number sectors, on common orbitals. The two differ by the ensemble ghost interaction G. We show that, for two determinants, the numbers of spin-orbitals gained and lost between them classify G before any calculation. G vanishes on every orbital set at pair rank one, has a fixed sign at pair rank two and whenever two or more spin-orbitals are only gained or only lost, and otherwise has an orbital-dependent sign. For larger ensembles, G vanishes on every orbital set when all pair covariances of the occupations vanish, and in the complete-basis limit only then. The same pairs add a covariance term to the orbital gradient and give the error of the chemical potential estimated from the ensemble Fock matrix. We implemented both methods in the eT program. The calculations give G = 0.24 Hartree at half transfer for the hexaamminecobalt(III/II) couple, 78-84% of the FON-UHF penalty for a fraction shared between the degenerate frontier orbitals of benzene, and the limit 1/(4R) for a hole shared between two stacked ethylene molecules.

summary: Geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) on unstructured polyhedral meshes reconstructs the interface orientation from the volume fractions of a stencil of neighbours; on irregular cells and in the presence of wisps it degrades, and the curvature built on it drives the parasitic currents of capillary flows. From the area and volume fractions, closed-form equations recover the interface normal and position of a cell, for the first time in VOF: the normal from one sum over the cell's own faces, the divergence theorem on the liquid sub-volume, and the plane's position from a second, without neighbours or iteration. Transported with the plane clipping, the ring normal, the same identity on the union of the cell's ring, stabilises the state and carries a sphere over 3.3 diameters bounded and conservative, first order in the face fractions as the clipping law predicts, at plicRDF's position and shape errors.
